row.name: Aston Valley Barrow Cemetery
row.description: The Aston Valley Barrow Cemetery, or Ashton Valley Barrow Cemetery, is a group of Bronze Age bowl barrow and bell barrow tumuli on the south facing edge of Codford Down on the west side of the valley of the Chitterne Brook, within the civil parish of Codford, in Wiltshire [1]. There were originally ten bowl barrows and a single bell barrow, but some of these have now been ploughed out: only the bell barrow and five bowl barrows survive [1]. The site lies in close proximity to Codford Circle, an Iron Age hillfort or enclosure some 2 km to the southeast, and Knook Castle, an Iron Age hillfort a similar distance to the northwest [1]. Excavations at the barrows have revealed many Bronze Age and some possible Saxon urned cremations and other interments [1]. The barrows were originally excavated by W.F. Cunnington in 1801, and recorded by Sir R. Colt-Hoare, with later excavations by the Reverend E.H. Steele in 1957; and with further correlations by Leslie Grinsell [1]. Some burials and items were left in place by Cunnington, but others are now preserved at the Wiltshire Museum in Devizes [1].

row.name: Bartlow Hills
row.description: Bartlow Hills is a Roman tumuli cemetery in Bartlow, Cambridgeshire [1]. The tallest barrow is 15 metres high, and is the largest Roman barrow north of the Alps [1]. The barrows date from the 1st or 2nd centuries AD [1]. Excavations were undertaken in the 19th century, discovering walled graves containing human cremains within glass vessels, which were stored in large wooden chests [1]. Decorated vessels in bronze, enamel, pottery and an iron folding chair were also found among other funerary goods [1].

row.name: Seahenge
row.description: Seahenge, also known as Holme I, was a prehistoric monument located in the village of Holme-next-the-Sea, near Old Hunstanton in the English county of Norfolk [1]. A timber circle with an upturned tree root in the centre, Seahenge, along with the nearby timber circle Holme II, was built in the spring-summer of 2049 BC [1]. The site consisted of an outer ring comprising 55 small split oak trunks forming a roughly circular enclosure around 7 by 6 metres [1]. Rather than being placed in individual holes, the timbers had been arranged around a circular construction trench [1]. Their split sides faced inwards and their bark faced outwards (with one exception where the opposite is the case) [1]. One of the trunks on the south western side had a narrow Y fork in it, permitting access to the central area [1]. Seahenge was originally constructed on a salt marsh, and over the centuries the area became a freshwater wetland, as an offshore barrier grew up, preventing sea water from getting access to the area around the circle [1].

row.name: Barreira Megalithic Complex
row.description: The Barreira Megalithic Complex is located in the Sintra municipality in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. Situated on a small wooded hill overlooking the village of Odrinhas, site of Roman ruins and an archaeological museum, it consists of about twenty menhirs and other monoliths or megaliths [1]. The site, which is assumed to be a dolmen or cromlech, contains mainly cylindrical stones of varying heights, with the largest being approximately four metres tall [1]. No carved or painted symbols have been detected, except for a few pairs of small circular cavities, possibly representing eyes [1]. A small number of items have been found to the west of the complex, including flints from the Lower Paleolithic, ceramic fragments and other items from the Neolithic period, and ceramic fragments from the Iron Age, suggesting that the site has been reused over time [1]. The complex was not identified as a megalithic site until 1961 when it was studied by Gil Estevam Miguéis Andrade and Eduardo Prescott Vicente [1].

row.name: Coventina
row.description: Dedications to Coventina and votive deposits were found in a walled area which had been built to contain the outflow from a spring now called "Coventina's Well" [1]. The well itself was a spring in a rectangular basin 2.6m x 2.4m in the centre of a walled enclosure 11.6m x 12.2m within a wall 0.9m thick [1]. The contents of the well included 13,487 coins from Mark Anthony to Gratian, a relief of three water nymphs, the head of a male statue, two dedication slabs to the goddess Coventina, ten altars to Coventina and Minerva, two clay incense burners, and a wide range of votive objects [1]. Excavation of the site revealed several inscribed altars, some with depictions of Coventina in typical Roman nymph form: reclining, partially clothed and associated with water [1]. At least ten inscriptions to Coventina are recorded from Carrawburgh [1]. Several stone altars contained dedications to Coventina as did two pottery incense burners [1].

row.name: Vale Maria do Meio Cromlech
row.description: The Vale Maria do Meio Cromlech is a megalithic stone circle situated in Évora district in the Alentejo region of Portugal [1]. It is believed to date back to the fifth millennium BCE or earlier [1]. The cromlech was identified in 1993 by a team of students from the University of Lisbon, led by Manuel Calado [1]. Excavations in 1995, sponsored by the local authority and led by Prof. Calado, identified 34 granite menhirs, which are predominantly oval in shape and have an average height of 1.74 meters [1]. Suggesting an astronomical purpose, the stones form an east-west elongated arch, which is about 37 meters long and 25 meters wide, with the largest monoliths being placed at the highest point of the site, to the west [1]. Engravings of circles, horseshoes and lunar crescents have been found on two of the menhirs, closely resembling engravings found on the Almendres Cromlech [1]. The arrangement of the menhirs suggested to the archaeologists that this monument was built in two distinct phases [1].

row.name: La Sufricaya
row.description: La Sufricaya is an archaeological site of the pre-Columbian Maya civilization, located in the Petén Basin region of present-day Guatemala [1]. The site is situated approximately 1.2 km (0.75 mi) west of the site of Holmul, and the relationship between these two sites during the Classic period occupations is a main focus of ongoing investigations [1].

row.name: Dun Vulan
row.description: Dun Vulan Broch (Scottish Gaelic: 'Dùn Mhùlan' or 'Dùn Mhaoilinn') is an Iron Age broch in South Uist, Scotland [1]. The site is now situated on an exposed promontory but was originally on a freshwater lake [1]. Dun Vulan is an Iron Age (c. 150–50 BC) broch located on the southern edge of the promontory; it is now protected as a sea wall [1]. Excavations revealed an oval-shaped broch with a maximum diameter of 19.5 metres, with walls surviving to 4.5 metres in height and 4 metres in width [1]. Between June 1991 and July 1996 Dun Vulan was excavated as part of the SEARCH (Sheffield Environmental and Archaeological Research Campaign in the Hebrides) Project [1]. The excavations suggested that there were no earlier structures predating the main structure on site [1].

row.name: Am Forsthofweg
row.description: The castellum or small fort nowadays called Am Forsthofweg was a Roman military camp of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes [1]. It received UNESCO World Heritage status in 2005 [1]. The fortification was located in the area of the current Bad Hönningen association of municipalities within the district of Neuwied in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany [1]. The fort was discovered in 1894 under the direction of Heinrich Jacobi, the local section commissioner of the Imperial Limes Commission, and examined in two excavation campaigns in 1894 and 1901 [1]. The Roman fortlet "Am Forsthofweg" is an almost square earthwork [1]. A rampart and a ditch 5 meters wide and 1.5 meters deep served as a first defense line [1]. With its only gate, the camp faced north, towards the Limes frontline [1]. A wooden construction of unknown function, covering around 45 square meters was found inside [1].

row.name: The Longstones
row.description: The Longstones are two standing stones, one of which is the remains of a prehistoric 'cove' of standing stones, at grid reference SU089693, close to Beckhampton in Avebury parish [1]. Two stones are visible, known as 'Adam' and 'Eve', although the latter is more likely to have been a stone that formed part of the Beckhampton Avenue that connected with Avebury [1]. Adam is the larger of the two stones, weighing an estimated 62 tons, and along with three others formed a four-sided cove [1]. Excavations carried out jointly by the Universities of Leicester, Newport and Southampton in 2000 revealed the socket holes for the other stones which were tightly placed close to Adam [1]. The cove had been open on its south-eastern side which faced towards the nearby South Street barrow, 130m away [1]. The other stones were removed in the post-medieval period by a local landowner [1]. Adam fell over in 1911 and was re-erected by Maud Cunnington in 1912, at the direction of the Wiltshire Archaeological Society [1]. She also found a Beaker inhumation of a middle-aged man buried close by the stone [1].

row.name: S'Argamassa Roman Fish Farm
row.description: S'Argamassa Roman Fish Farm can be found 2.8 miles eastwards along the coast from the town of Santa Eulària des Riu on the Spanish island of Ibiza [1]. The Romans built this fish farm and connecting aqueduct following their occupation of the island in 146 BC [1]. The conduit is built from large limestone slabs with a channel carved into the top surface [1]. At the end of the run of the aqueduct close to the shoreline there are the remains of rectangular structures which were once the fermenting tanks for the production of the garum [1]. On completion of the process the sauce was packed into enormous earthenware storage jars called amphoras, also produced locally, and exported to all parts of the empire [1].

row.name: Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo
row.description: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos [1]. Dating back to the early Neolithic, and of a considerable weight and size, it has a cylindrical shape and a decorative spiral-like engraving that's faintly discernible [1]. It was part of a group of eight other similar monuments, of which just one is still standing in its original location [1]. The rest were taken by Lagos's city hall for preservation [1]. Just like other Menhirs found in the Algarve, the Cabeça do Rochedo Menir did not serve funerary purposes, and the end it served is still debated [1]. The monument is located at a hill just outside of Portelas, 6 km north of Lagos [1].

row.name: Priddy Circles
row.description: Priddy Circles are a linear arrangement of four circular earthwork enclosures near the village of Priddy on the Mendip Hills in Somerset [1]. The circles have been listed as Scheduled Ancient Monuments, and described as 'probable Neolithic ritual or ceremonial monuments similar to a henge' [1]. The enclosures range in diameter from 185 to 194 m [1]. Three of the circles are closely spaced in a nearly straight line, while the fourth is 350 m to the north and somewhat out of line with the other three [1]. The total arrangement is spread over roughly 1.2 km [1]. The four circles each consist of a flat circular area surrounded by a bank and external ditch enclosure with more than one entrance [1].

row.name: Quispiguanca
row.description: Quispiguanca was a royal estate of the Inca emperor Huayna Capac (c. 1464–1525 CE) [1]. The ruins of the estate are located in the northern part of the present-day town of Urubamba, Peru at an elevation of 2,910 metres [1]. The estate of Huayna Capac extended for 15 kilometres up and down the Sacred Valley [1]. The archaeological remains consist of a terrace, a well—preserved wall, gatehouses on the east side of the site, and several structures in poor condition in the northern third of the site [1]. Most of the construction is of fitted stonework, although some adobe and plaster were also used [1]. The original palace compound was rectangular and measured within its walls 189 metres north-south and 125 metres east-west [1]. The northernmost part of the compound consists of agricultural terraces and the stone foundation of a great hall, measuring 14 metres by 44 metres [1]. The Spanish conquistador of the Inca Empire, Francisco Pizarro, appropriated the estate of Huayna Capac as his encomienda in the 1530s [1].

row.name: North Bersted Man
row.description: The North Bersted Man is the modern name given to a warrior found in a burial at excavations by the Thames Valley Archaeological services made in 2008 near North Bersted [1]. The burial contained an exceptional set of objects [1]. It was found within settlement remains that date from the Iron Age to the Roman period [1]. The burial of the North Bersted Man dates to the first century BC [1]. The most remarkable object was the helmet of the warrior [1]. It was adorned with two crests that once ran across the top of the helmet and down its back [1].

row.name: Llyn Cerrig Bach
row.description: Llyn Cerrig Bach is a small lake located between Rhosneigr and Valley in the west of Anglesey [1]. Whilst it is not one of the largest lakes on the island (around 1.8 acres), its claim to fame is the group of over 150 Iron Age metal objects discovered there in 1942, apparently placed in the lake as votive offerings [1]. These finds are considered to be one of the most important collections of La Tène style metalwork, or Early Celtic art discovered in the British Isles, and the most important in Wales [1]. The discovery was made by William Owen Roberts, head groundsman of RAF Valley, when ground was being cleared for a runway extension [1]. This involved spreading peat over the sandy ground, and the items were discovered during the extraction of peat from the Cors yr Ynys bog on the southern margin of Llyn Cerrig Bach [1]. The first object to be found was an iron gang chain, used for slaves [1].

row.name: Sidrón Cave
row.description: The Sidrón Cave is a non-carboniferous limestone karst cave system located in the Piloña municipality of Asturias where Paleolithic rock art and the fossils of more than a dozen Neanderthals were found [1]. The total length of this huge complex is approximately 3,700 m, which contains a central hall of 200 m length and the Neanderthal fossil site, called the Ossuary Gallery, which is 28 m long and 12 m wide [1]. In 1994, human remains were found accidentally in the cave [1]. They were initially suspected to be from the Spanish Civil War because Republican fighters used to hide there; however, later analysis shows that the remains actually belong to Neanderthals [1]. Researchers recovered more than 2500 hominin fossil elements from the site [1]. The minimum number of individuals from Sidrón Cave is 13 [1]. The age of these remains of three men, three adolescent boys, four women, and three infants has been estimated to about 49,000 years [1]. The first sequencing of the Neanderthal Y chromosome was successfully completed from a specimen from Sidrón Cave [1].

row.name: Lisnadarragh Wedge Tomb
row.description: Lisnadarragh Wedge Tomb is a prehistoric site, a wedge tomb about 16 kilometres west of Carrickmacross, in County Monaghan near the border with County Cavan [1]. The tomb at Lisnadarragh is aligned roughly north-east to south-west, and measures about 4.5 by 2 metres [1]. The sides of the tomb are defined by 20 orthostats, which decrease in size from south-west to north-east, the largest, at the entrance, being of height 1.8 metres [1].

row.name: Taliata
row.description: Taliata was a Roman town and fort located near the present town of Donji Milanovac in eastern Serbia [1]. It is included in the Tabula Peutingeriana [1]. The fort of 134 × 126 m was built as part of the Roman Moesian Limes frontier system of linked forts along the Danube [1]. Domitian replaced the wood and earth walls by stone walls in 87 AD before Domitian's Dacian War [1]. It was completely restored in the second half of the 3rd century [1]. In the 4th c. protruding semicircular corner-towers were added [1]. An early Christian basilica was discovered on the site [1].

row.name: Xrobb l-Għaġin Temple
row.description: Xrobb l-Għaġin Temple is a ruined megalithic temple in Xrobb l-Għaġin, limits of Marsaxlokk, Malta [1]. After being identified in 1913, the site was excavated between 1914 and 1915 [1]. It was believed to have been largely destroyed by coastal erosion later on in the century, but investigations carried out in 2015 revealed that the remains of the temple still survive, along with a previously unrecorded megalithic structure nearby [1]. Xrobb l-Għaġin Megalithic Site had a typical temple plan with two apses and a central niche [1]. The earliest remains in the area date back to around 4000 BC, but the temple itself was built between 3600 and 3000 BC, during the Ġgantija phase of Maltese prehistory [1]. The site was excavated by Zammit and A. V. Laferla between December 1914 and January 1915, revealing the core of a megalithic temple [1]. A clay bowl, some slingstones and a decorated slab which formed part of a niche were retrieved during these excavations and they are now displayed at the National Museum of Archaeology in Valletta [1].

row.name: Uzun oba
row.description: Uzun Oba is an archaeological excavation site in Azerbaijan [1]. It is located on the right bank of the Nakhchivançay near the village of Aşağı Uzunoba in the Babək district [1]. The site was investigated during excavations of the international archaeological expedition Azerbaijan-France in 2015 [1]. Vali Baxşəliyev and Catherine Marro were the leaders of the expedition [1]. During the excavation, painted ceramic pieces from the V millennium BC came to light [1]. Such ancient finds are very rare for the region [1].

row.name: Tumlehed Rock Painting
row.description: The Tumlehed rock painting is a prehistoric rock art pictograph site, located in Tumlehed on the island of Hisingen, Gothenburg Municipality [1]. It is the southernmost recorded rock painting in Sweden and one of few found in the western parts of the country [1]. A minor excavation was carried out in 1985 of the area next to the painting, but no significant finds were made [1]. Situated on a steep cliff face, covering about 2 x 2 meters, it depicts a number of figures, among them four ships, four fish, a large deer, wave-like patterns, and some undetermined shapes [1]. The painting was made with a mixture of red ochre and a binder which through bonding with the rock has survived the years [1].

row.name: Watling Temple
row.description: Watling Temple is the name given to the remains of a temple within a Roman town next to the modern A2 road in Newington, near Sittingbourne in Kent, England [1]. The town was rediscovered in 2019 during an archaeological dig covering 18 acres that found iron furnaces and pottery kilns as part of a manufacturing site, a Roman temple, a 7 metres wide Roman road and late Iron Age remains dating from 30 BC [1]. The Roman road Watling Street runs through the village of Newington, and the newly discovered road predates it and takes an alternative route [1].

row.name: El Temblor
row.description: El Temblor is an archaeological site in Petén Department, Guatemala which was once the location of a settlement of the Maya civilization [1]. First recorded in 1974 by Ian Graham of Harvard University's Peabody Museum, the site represents a medium-sized and compact settlement about 18 kilometres (11 mi) south-south-east of the ruined Mayan city of Tikal and about 13 kilometres (8.1 mi) north-east of the ruins of Ixlu [1]. It is situated in a wooded area called Paso del Carmen [1]. The ruins at El Temblor consist of at least three groups of collapsed structures or platforms on a north-south axis [1]. The northernmost group, designated as Group A, is clustered in a wooded hilltop and includes a pyramid standing over 10 metres (33 ft) high [1]. A damaged stela stands east of the pyramid [1]. Group B is located in a lower and flatter area to the south and includes at least five mounds or platforms [1]. Group C is located further south along the site's main axis and comprises eight structures on a hill, possibly representing temples and palaces [1].

row.name: Venado Beach
row.description: Venado Beach is part of the Gran Coclé culture [1]. This site is notable for its large number and variety of burials and grave goods, especially those with offerings objects of gold and evidence for human sacrifice [1]. Venado Beach was once within the target area used by Fort Kobbe, about 10 miles from the 16th century Spanish settlement of Old Panama [1]. It was first discovered by the U.S. Navy in 1948 while bulldozing off the topsoil in order to enrich the lawns of the 15th Naval District [1]. The site was excavated in the late 1940s and early 1950s [1]. The skeletal remains of a total of 369 individuals were found extended across the Mangopobre Valley [1]. Excavators found many burials in ceramic urns [1].

row.name: Vespasian's Camp
row.description: Vespasian's Camp is an Iron Age hillfort just west of the town of Amesbury, Wiltshire [1]. The hillfort is less than 3 kilometres from the Neolithic and Bronze Age site of Stonehenge, and was built on a hill next to the Stonehenge Avenue; it has the River Avon on its southern side and the A303 road on its northern edge [1]. The site is a scheduled monument and lies within the boundaries of the Stonehenge World Heritage Site [1]. The earthworks were named "Vespasian's Camp" in the 16th century by William Camden, an Elizabethan antiquarian and historian, during a tour of the area [1]. Although the Roman general Vespasian, who was later Roman emperor from 69 to 79 CE, campaigned through Wessex after the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 CE, there is no evidence to suggest he came to this hillfort or had any military base here [1]. Aligned from north to south, the hillfort is 730 m long and 374 m wide at its southern end, narrowing to 100 m wide at the north [1]. It encloses an area of some 14 ha [1].

row.name: Pod
row.description: Pod is an archeological site in the municipality of Bugojno, Bosnia and Herzegovina [1]. It is a prehistoric settlement and hill fort located about 40 metres (130 ft) above the bed of the river Poričnica, a tributary of the Vrbas, on a slope of Mountain Koprivnica above the main road leading from Bugojno to Gornji Vakuf, in the settlement of Čipuljić, today an integral part of Bugojno [1]. Stratified materials from Pod defined Central Bosnian cultural group of the late Bronze Age [1]. Archaeological excavation was undertaken there led by Branka Raunig in 1973 [1].

row.name: La Muerta
row.description: La Muerta is a Maya archaeological site in the northern Petén region of Guatemala, located between the sites of El Mirador and El Tintal [1]. It is located on a promontory 3.5 kilometres south of the El Tigre complex of El Mirador, and it is considered a satellite of that city [1]. La Muerta was inhabited during the Early to Late Classic Period [1]. La Muerta was investigated by archaeologist Richard D. Hansen in the 1980s [1]. The site is divided into North and South Groups, located approximately 400 metres apart [1]. Eleven residential areas have been identified within these two groups [1]. Structure A1 is a temple with a north-facing stairway [1]. Monument 1 is a sculptured stela that was found in the North Group [1].

row.name: Klekkende Høj
row.description: Klekkende Høj is a megalithic tomb on the island of Møn in Denmark [1]. The tomb is believed to date from the Neolithic Age, ca. 3500-2800 BC, and is one of the best preserved of more than 100 burial mounds on the island [1]. The tomb is a passage grave, which means that the central chamber within the mound is reached by a connecting passage [1]. Klekkende Høj is unusual in that there are two entrance passages running approximately parallel to each other, facing east [1]. Within the mound is a central space running approximately north-south, which is divided through the centre by two large stones [1]. The tomb was excavated in 1797 by Antoine de Bosc de la Calmette, who was governor of the island [1]. Inside were a considerable number of human remains, flint weapons, clay vessels and amber jewellery [1].

row.name: Ashdown Forest
row.description: Ashdown Forest contains over 570 archaeological sites preserved by heathland conditions and minimal ploughing [1]. The earliest evidence is a stone hand axe found near Gills Lap, dated to approximately 50,000 years ago [1] [2]. The site features Bronze Age round barrows, Iron Age enclosures, prehistoric field systems, and Roman iron workings [2]. Medieval and post-medieval pillow mounds for rabbit breeding survive across the forest [1]. Notably, military kitchen mounds between Camp Hill and Nutley from 1793 are among only a handful surviving in the United Kingdom [1].

row.name: Longforth Farm
row.description: Longforth Farm, on the outskirts of Wellington, Somerset, England, is the site of a Bronze Age landscape and an extensive medieval structure [1]. The previously unknown site, which covers 0.4 hectares, was uncovered during excavations in 2013 prior to the building of 500 new houses by Bloor Homes [1]. The stone foundations, which are covered in decorated tiles are laid out around courtyards [1]. The remains of roof slates and glazed ceramic roof tiles have also been found [1]. The floor tiles are similar to those at Glastonbury Abbey, while the pottery finds have been dated to between the 12th and 14th centuries [1].

row.name: Penrhos Feilw Standing Stones
row.description: The Penrhos Feilw Standing Stones are a pair of standing stones on Holy Island west of Anglesey in north-west Wales [1]. They are thought to date from the Bronze Age but their origins and purpose are unclear [1]. The stones are located behind the farmhouse of Plas Meilw, some 2 km southwest of Holyhead and a similar distance south of Holyhead Mountain [1]. The exposed part of each stone is about 3 m high and 1 m broad at the base, but only about 20 cm thick [1]. They are situated about 3 m apart on an open grassy place above Porth Dafarch between two low hills [1]. They are aligned along their long axes in a northeasterly/southwesterly direction [1].

row.name: Hypogeum of Cala Sant Vicenç
row.description: The Hypogeum of Cala Sant Vicenç is a set of caves in Cala Sant Vicenç, on the Spanish island of Mallorca [1]. It dates back to the Bronze Age (1,700—1,500 BC) [1]. Today, eight caves are visible, though when they were studied by Wilfrid James Hemp, there were fifteen [1]. Some features of the caves are modern [1].

row.name: Mogilan Mound
row.description: The Mogilan mound or Mogilanska mound is a burial mound in the center of Vratsa, Bulgaria [1]. During excavations in 1965–66, 3 tombs were found in it, built of stone [1]. One of them - tomb No 2, was found intact and yielded a rich treasure-trove of artifacts [1]. Tomb No 2 consists of an anteroom and a chamber [1]. In the chamber there was a funeral with many treasures: a gold wreath and earrings, a gilded silver knee pad with an image of the great mother goddess, a set of magic figurines, as well as different vessels and objects made of silver, bronze and ceramics [1]. The other two tombs were looted in antiquity and yielded only a small amount of random objects – a gold and silver jug and others [1]. It is likely that prominent members of the ruler dynasty of the Triballi were buried in those tombs in the 4th century BC [1].

row.name: Dulan Site
row.description: The Dulan Site (traditional Chinese: 都蘭遺址; simplified Chinese: 都兰遗址; pinyin: Dōulán Yízhǐ) is an archaeological site in Dulan Village, Donghe Township, Taitung County, Taiwan [1]. During Japanese rule of Taiwan, a rectangular stony coffin was excavated in the area [1]. Further investigation by Academia Sinica led to the discovery of a giant stone pile [1]. The site and objects date back to 3,000 years ago [1]. It is now considered a cultural heritage and third grade historical site [1]. The area is divided into two areas, which are the stony coffin area and the stony wall area [1].

row.name: Na Nova
row.description: Na Nova is a Spanish Iron Age Talaiotic settlement located on the island of Mallorca [1]. Although its entirety is highly altered, it has been designated a Bien de Interés Cultural [1]. Its most characteristic structure is the talaiot, a tower-shaped megalithic structure which is in good conditions [1]. The talaiot's diameter is 12 metres on the outside and 6 metres on the inside [1]. It is more than 2 metres high and it preserves five courses of huge stones in its best preserved parts [1]. The inside is full of rubblestones, but the polylithic column still stands, as does the entrance with its stone lintel [1]. The rest of the structures are partially razed and covered with more rubble, and have not been satisfactorily identified [1]. The site was densely and totally covered with bushes and trees until its first cleaning in 2016 and 2017 [1].

row.name: Lang Rongrien Rock Shelter
row.description: The Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers who lived at the Lang Rongrien rock shelter used the site as a temporary habitation site [1]. The oldest use for the rock shelter was as a campground for hunters in the late Pleistocene epoch [1]. The excavated areas of the Lang Rongrien rock shelter have been divided into ten stratigraphic layers, or cultural deposit layers [1]. The eighth and ninth layers are similar to each other, with charcoal remains, stone artifacts and flakes, and animal bones that are scattered about among these layers [1]. The oldest pieces of charcoal found in the lower most layers where human habitation is seen have been dated to around 39,000 years ago [1]. Charcoal pieces from the upper layers have been dated to about 9,000 years ago [1].

row.name: Kutikina Cave
row.description: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness, a World Heritage Area in the Australian state of Tasmania [1]. Originally referred to as Fraser Cave, it was important in the establishment of the antiquity and range of Aboriginal occupation in Tasmania during the Pleistocene [1]. The cave was discovered in 1977 by geomorphology student Kevin Keirnan and investigated by a team led by archeologists Don Ranson and Rhys Jones in the 1980s [1]. The cave has important archaeological deposits relating to human occupation in the Pleistocene, with evidence of wallaby hunting at a time the landscape was an open tundra and it was the most southerly human occupation in the world during the last ice age [1].

row.name: Margery Hill
row.description: Margery Hill is a 546-metre hill on the Howden Moors in South Yorkshire, England [1]. It lies towards the northern boundary of the Peak District National Park, between Langsett Reservoir to the northeast and Howden Reservoir to the southwest [1]. The area is managed by the National Trust as part of their High Peak Estate [1]. Peat near the summit cairn has been dated to a uniform age of about 3,500 years old, indicating that it was constructed rather than natural; it is believed to have been part of a Bronze Age burial mound [1]. The area has been designated a Scheduled Ancient Monument by English Heritage [1]. Margery Hill is the highest marked point within the boundaries of the City of Sheffield [1].

row.name: Borough Hill Roman Villa
row.description: Borough Hill Roman villa is located on the north tip of Borough Hill, a prominent hill near the town of Daventry in Northamptonshire [1]. The villa’s remains lie within the ramparts of an Iron Age fortress which covers the summit of the hill [1]. The remains of the Roman villa were discovered in 1823 by the historian and archaeologist George Baker [1]. The remains were not fully excavated until 1852 when local historian Beriah Botfield thoroughly excavated and recorded the site [1]. Botfield’s excavations revealed a large range of rooms which ran from north to south, part of which was a bath suite [1]. It was deduced that the buildings were built over a period of time and that the northern rooms are later additions [1]. The earliest parts of the villa were built in the early years of the Roman occupation [1]. The villa consisted of a single storey and was constructed from the local marlstone (sandstone), infilled with rubble [1].

row.name: El Azuzul
row.description: El Azuzul is an Olmec archaeological site in Veracruz, Mexico, a few kilometers south of the San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán complex and generally considered contemporary with it (perhaps 1100 to 800 BCE) [1]. Named for the ranch on which it is located, El Azuzul is part of the Loma del Zapote complex [1]. The site occupies the higher elevations north of the confluence of two ancient river courses, a part of the Coatzacoalcos River system [1]. It is upstream of the monumental earthworks at Potrero Nuevo, which is part of the San Lorenzo complex [1]. El Azuzul is best known for two pairs of monumental sculptures, now on exhibit at the Xalapa Museum of Anthropology, Xalapa [1]. These statues were found on the south side of the large pyramid/hill on the site, intact and apparently undisturbed since they were placed there in Pre-Classic times [1]. The first pair of statues, described as "some of the greatest masterpieces of Olmec art", are nearly identical seated human figures [1].

row.name: Tune Stone
row.description: The Tune stone is a runestone written circa 200–450 AD [1]. It is written in the Elder Futhark script, and its language is Proto-Norse [1]. It was discovered in 1627 in the church yard wall of the church in Tune, Østfold, Norway [1]. Today it is housed in the Norwegian Museum of Cultural History in Oslo [1]. The Tune stone is possibly the oldest Norwegian attestation of burial rites, inheritance, and beer [1]. The stone has inscriptions on two sides, called side A and side B. Side A consists of an inscription of two lines, and side B consists of an inscription of three lines [1]. The runic inscription was first interpreted by Sophus Bugge in 1903 and Carl Marstrander in 1930, but the full text was not interpreted convincingly until 1981 by Ottar Grønvik in his book Runene på Tunesteinen [1].

row.name: Harrow Way
row.description: The Harrow Way is another name for the "Old Way", an ancient trackway in the south of England, dated by archaeological finds to 600–450 BC, but probably in existence since the Stone Age [1]. The Old Way ran from Seaton in Devon to Dover [1]. The eastern part of the Harrow Way from Farnham, Surrey, later known as the Pilgrims' Way, runs on or parallel to the North Downs Way National trail [1]. The Harrow Way can be traced from Rochester and alternative Channel ports on the Straits of Dover [1]. In Dorset, the Harrow Way can be traced through the villages of Halstock and Corscombe, where it is known as Common Lane [1]. At the Halstock end, a short length was realigned to form the access for a Roman villa (which was built on the site of a late Iron Age farmstead) [1].

row.name: Kordin Temples
row.description: The Kordin Temples are a group of megalithic temples on Corradino Heights in Paola [1]. The temples are located on a plateau overlooking the Grand Harbour, originally called Kortin during the Order of St. John and now Kordin or Corradino [1]. Kordin III is the only temple on Corradino whose remains have survived [1]. The Kordin III complex consists of two temples [1]. The larger one has a standard 3-apse plan, typical of Ġgantija phase design [1]. The temple has a concave facade, with the forecourt and entrance passage to the central court being stone-paved [1]. This stone paving is unique to Kordin III, as this has not been found in any other temples of Malta [1]. The first part of the temple is believed to have been built in around 3700 BC, during the Mġarr phase [1].

row.name: St Breock Downs Monolith
row.description: St Breock Downs Monolith is the largest and heaviest prehistoric Menhir in Cornwall [1]. It stands on the summit of St Breock Downs [1]. The stone is made from the local Devonian shale which has extensive feldspar veining, and it is estimated to weigh around 16.5 tonnes [1]. It is 4.92 metres long and stands to a height of just over 3 metres above ground level [1]. It stands on a low stone mound or cairn with a diameter of around 10 metres [1]. It is believed to be Late Neolithic or Early Bronze Age (around 2500-1500 BC) [1]. It fell over in 1945, and was re-erected in 1956 after a small excavation had been carried out [1]. The excavation showed that the stone stood in a setting of quartz pebbles below which were two small hollows [1].

row.name: Templebryan Stone Circle
row.description: Templebryan Stone Circle (also known as The Druid's Temple) is a stone circle, located 2.5 km north of Clonakilty, County Cork, Ireland [1]. Close by lies an Early Christian site [1]. Today there are only four upright stones of the original nine [1]. Nearby are the remains of a small, ruined church beside another upright stone with a bullaun [1].

row.name: Witham Shield
row.description: The Witham Shield is an Iron Age decorative bronze shield facing of La Tène style, dating from about the 4th century BC [1]. The shield was discovered in the River Witham in the vicinity of Washingborough and Fiskerton in Lincolnshire, England in 1826 [1]. The shield is now in the British Museum [1]. The bronze facings show evidence of having been reworked [1]. Originally a leather silhouette of a long-legged wild boar would have been riveted to the shield around the central dome, as indicated by small rivet holes and staining of the shield [1].

row.name: Carn Euny
row.description: Carn Euny is an archaeological site near Sancreed, on the Penwith peninsula in Cornwall [1]. It consists of evidence of both Iron Age and post-Iron Age settlement, with excavation on the site showing activity at Carn Euny as early as the Neolithic period [1]. The first timber huts there were built about 500 BC, and 400–500 years later were replaced by stone huts, the remains of which are still visible [1]. Carn Euny is best known for the well-preserved state of the large fogou, an underground passageway, which is more than 65 feet long [1]. This fogou runs just below the surface of the ground and is roofed with massive stone slabs [1]. The site was abandoned late in the Roman period [1].

row.name: Slate Hill Settlement
row.description: Slate Hill Settlement is an archaeological site in Northumberland, England, near the village of Bolam and about 7 miles west of Morpeth [1]. The site, a defended settlement dating from the Iron Age, is a scheduled monument [1]. The site is regarded as an example of a type of defended settlement of the Iron Age, first constructed in the 7th to 5th centuries BC in the northern uplands of what is now England, sometimes located on hilltops [1]. On Slate Hill there are four concentric ramparts, terraced on the sloping hillside, in a semicircle forming on the north and west sides of an enclosure; quarrying has affected the east side where one rampart remains [1]. The ramparts, of stone and earth, are about 5 metres (16 ft) wide and 1.4 metres (4 ft 7 in) high [1]. On the south side a steep slope provides defence [1]. The enclosure within the defences is about 98 metres west to east and 62 metres north to south [1].

row.name: Six Hills
row.description: The Six Hills are a collection of Roman barrows situated alongside the old Great North Road on Six Hills Common in Stevenage, Hertfordshire [1]. They are classed as a Scheduled Ancient Monument and are protected by law [1]. They form the largest surviving Roman barrow group in England [1]. For almost two thousand years, travellers along the Roman road that eventually became the Great North Road have passed these six large mounds [1].

row.name: Markahirka
row.description: Markahirka or Marka Hirka is an archaeological site with cave paintings and stone tombs on a mountain of the same name in Peru [1]. It is located in the Ancash Region, Huari Province, in the districts of Cajay and Masin [1]. It is situated at a height of 3,580 metres [1]. Markahirka is also a good viewpoint with views into the Puchka valley and to the towns of Huari and Huachis [1].

row.name: Graves of Sainte-Colombe-sur-Seine
row.description: The Graves of Sainte-Colombe-sur-Seine are several burial mounds dating from the 6th century BC [1]. The burials are associated with the Iron Age Hallstatt culture [1]. In the 19th century they were excavated at the request of Napoleon III, revealing elite wagon burials containing gold jewellery and prestigious imported artefacts [1]. The first to be excavated, located at La Garenne, provided a magnificent bronze lebes of Etruscan origin [1]. In another, at La Butte, gold bracelets and earrings were discovered in the grave of a woman who had been laid to rest on a luxurious iron-clad funerary wagon [1]. In the middle of the 20th century René Joffroy postulated that the elites buried under the tumuli of La Butte and La Garenne had Mont Lassois as their place of residence [1].

row.name: Koviljkin grad
row.description: Koviljkin grad or Koviljka is a name for archaeological ruins close to Banja Koviljača in the Loznica district of western Serbia [1]. The ruins are of a Roman town, which may have been named Gensis; the name has never been confirmed [1]. It is located on the top of a hill, and the remains of the walls spread about 150 metres around it [1]. At the time of the Roman Empire, the river Drina flowed underneath this settlement, and it is believed that there was a Roman river harbour [1]. The site has not been completely explored by archaeologists [1].

row.name: Broch of Culswick
row.description: The Broch of Culswick is an unexcavated coastal broch in the Shetland Islands of Scotland [1]. Much rubble has fallen into the centre [1]. This broch has a massive triangular lintel stone over the entrance, which is partly filled with rubble [1]. Drawings by Low in 1774 and Skene in 1805 reveal that the structure survived very well up to those dates [1]. The Broch of Culswick is located a kilometre west of Culswick in the parish of Sandsting [1]. It is on top of a steep, smooth knoll near cliffs and the sea [1]. The main entrance is clearly visible but debris nearly fills the passage [1]. A "guard cell" was visible to the right of the main entrance [1].

row.name: Cornalvo Dam
row.description: The Cornalvo Dam is a Roman gravity dam built to supply water to the Roman colonia of Emerita Augusta, capital of the Roman province of Lusitania [1]. It was built in the 1st–2nd century AD as part of the infrastructure which supplied water [1]. The dam is part of the Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida, which is one of the largest and most extensive archaeological sites in Spain and that was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1993 [1].

row.name: Lapa de Gargantáns
row.description: The Lapa de Gargantáns is a menhir located in the Galician municipality of Moraña, dated between 3000–2000 BC and discovered in 1958 [1]. Several petroglyphs are engraved on its surface [1]. However, its exact function is unknown, and some archaeologists associate it with funerary, religious or commemorative signs, or ancient territorial boundaries between tribes [1].

row.name: Ali Murad Mound
row.description: The Ali Murad Mound is an archaeological site situated at Johi Tehsil, in Dadu District of Sindh, Pakistan [1]. The site was explored as well as named by archaeologist N. G. Majumdar [1]. It is located 20 miles from Dadu towards the southwest [1]. It is eight miles from Ghazi Shah Mound and 14 miles to the south of Johi town [1]. At the top of the mound, an ancient hamlet was discovered surrounded by defensive walls built with stone blocks [1].

row.name: Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications
row.description: The Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications, a huge Iron Age hill fort, sometimes but not always considered an oppidum, comprising over 9 kilometres of ditches and ramparts enclosing approximately 300 hectares of land, are situated in Richmondshire, North Yorkshire, England [1]. The site is a scheduled monument [1]. The fortifications are located 8 miles north of the town of Richmond and 10 miles south west of Darlington [1]. Rising to a height of almost 5 metres in places, the ramparts completely surround the village of Stanwick St John and form one of the largest Iron Age settlements in Britain, in extent if not necessarily in population [1]. Stanwick was the site of Sir Mortimer Wheeler's last major archaeological excavation in Britain, which he carried out over the summers of 1951 and 1952 [1]. Amongst Wheeler's most famous finds at Stanwick were an Iron Age sword, unusually still in its well-preserved ash wood scabbard, and the nearby skull of a severed head [1].

row.name: La Amelia
row.description: La Amelia is a Pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site near Itzan, in the lower Pasión River region of the Petén Department of Guatemala [1]. La Amelia was a subordinate site in the Classic Period Petexbatún kingdom of Mutal that was first ruled from Dos Pilas and then from Aguateca [1]. The site is located to the northwest of Dos Pilas, and may have originally been called B'ahlam [1]. The occupational history of La Amelia appears to have been brief and limited to the Late Classic [1]. In AD 802 the last known ruler of the kingdom, Tan Te' K'inich, supervised a ritual conducted by the ruler of La Amelia, Lachan K'awiil Ajaw Bot [1]. Lachan K'awiil Ajaw Bot, the local La Amelia king, is depicted on La Amelia Panel 2, dated to AD 804 and continued to raise monuments at the site [1]. La Amelia is a small site covering an area of approximately 0.74 square kilometres [1].

row.name: Square Peristyle
row.description: The Square Peristyle is the modern name for a structure on the east side of the Ancient Agora of Athens, which was among the largest peristyles built in Classical Greece [1]. Construction began around 300 BC, but was abandoned ca. 285-275 BC, leaving the structure unfinished [1]. It probably served as Athens' law courts at the beginning of the Hellenistic period, but fell out of use [1]. In the early second century BC the building was demolished and the material was reused in South Stoa II, on the southern side of the Agora [1]. The Stoa of Attalos was subsequently built over the top of its foundations [1]. Traces of the structure were revealed by American excavations in the 1950s, but were covered over shortly thereafter when the Stoa of Attalos was rebuilt [1].

row.name: Harhoog
row.description: The Harhoog is a dolmen, a rectangular megalithic tomb from the Funnelbeaker culture, located near Keitum on the island of Sylt in Schleswig-Holstein [1]. The megalithic Harhoog burial chambers were originally located near the mud-flats between Keitum and Tinnum [1]. The stones were moved to the area near the Tipkenhoog on the coast near Keitum in 1954, when Sylt Airport was under development [1]. The chambers contain parallel and transverse sections [1]. The graves at Harhoog are dated to the Neolithic and belonged to ancient settlements of the island's Funnelbeaker culture, probably around 3000 BC [1]. Harhoog dolmen is an extended dolmen, under Ernst Sprockhoff's six-category classification; the other five types are simple dolmen, great dolmen, passage grave, long barrows (without a burial chamber) and cist [1].

row.name: Roman Baths of Toledo
row.description: The Roman baths of Toledo or Roman thermae of Amador de los Ríos are ruins of Roman thermae located in the city of Toledo in Castile-La Mancha, Spain [1]. The baths can be seen as part of the system of supplying clean water to the city (then known by the Latin name of Toletum) [1]. From the scale of the surviving infrastructure, they are assumed to have been a public facility [1]. As regards chronology, the remains correspond to a period between the end of the 1st century and mid-2nd century CE [1]. The location of the baths at Amador de los Ríos square is high above the River Tagus [1]. In Roman times water was supplied from one of the river's tributaries and entered the city via an aqueduct about 80m above the Tajo [1]. There was a storage system using large cisterns [1].

row.name: Makra Stoa
row.description: The Makra Stoa was built during the time of Pericles [1]. It was also known as the Alphitopolis Stoa, from the Greek word alphita (barley flour) [1]. The Stoa was a long building which was used for the storage of imported cereals, mainly barley and wheat [1]. The cereals were then transported to the main city of Athens for consumption [1]. The Stoa also supplied the Athenian fleet of triremes and, during times of shortage, supplied the people directly [1]. The Stoa had an open facade and colonnade on one side and on the other side had shops made up of rectangular rooms [1]. The rooms alternated between small and large sizes and each shop had a space for supplying cereals and a grain storage area [1].

row.name: Roman Ruins of Creiro
row.description: The Roman ruins of Creiro are situated in the Arrábida Natural Park above Creiro Beach in the Setúbal District of Portugal [1]. They are ruins of a fish-salting factory and Roman baths, dating back to the days when the province of Lusitania formed part of the Roman Empire [1]. The factory at Creiro was one of the smaller but older production units for salted and pickled fish and fish sauces that were exported throughout the Empire in specially designed amphorae [1]. The ruins were first identified by the archaeologist António Inácio Marques da Costa in 1907 [1]. However, he provided no detailed information about the site and it was not until 1964 when his unpublished manuscripts were discovered that the nature of the site was officially known [1]. It was only in 1987 that the first archaeological excavation was carried out, by the Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology of Setúbal District, led by Carlos Tavares da Silva [1].

row.name: Artificial Caves of Alapraia
row.description: The Artificial caves of Alapraia constitute a prehistoric necropolis formed by four subterranean tombs or hypogea that were created by excavating marlstone rock using stone tools [1]. They are situated in the centre of the suburb of Alapraia in Estoril, Lisbon District, Portugal and are believed to date back to the last quarter of the 4th Millennium BCE and to have been used as a necropolis for over one thousand years [1]. All the caves had the same system of construction, consisting of a long corridor or vestibule for access, with a circular chamber at the end with a skylight at the top, protected by slabs [1]. This is believed to have made possible the placement of bodies into the chamber, when occupancy levels no longer allowed access through the corridor [1]. Cave 1 is 19 m long and was first described by the geologist F. de Paula e Oliveira in 1889 [1]. A spherical chamber has a diameter of 6.2 metres and a height of 2.8 metres in the middle [1].

row.name: Castle Dykes Henge
row.description: Castle Dykes Henge is a Class I Neolithic henge earthwork in the Yorkshire Dales National Park in North Yorkshire, England, situated between the villages of Aysgarth and Thornton Rust [1]. It consists of a roughly circular bank approximately 87 yards (80 m) in diameter with an internal ditch [1]. It is reported that excavation work took place in 1908, though there is little physical evidence of this as the henge appears to be mostly intact [1].

row.name: Pannonian Limes
row.description: The Pannonian Limes is part of the old Roman fortified frontier known as the Danubian Limes that runs for approximately 420 km from the Roman camp of Klosterneuburg in the Vienna Basin in Austria to the castrum in Singidunum in present-day Serbia [1]. The garrisons of these camps protected the Pannonian provinces against attacks from the north from the time of Augustus to the beginning of the 5th century [1]. The Danubian limes was one of the most turbulent regions in the European part of the Roman Empire and, during more than 400 years of Roman rule, Pannonia was one of its most important provinces, especially after the abandonment of Dacia Traiana in 271 AD, because from that point on, the pressure of migrating peoples on this section of the limes increased still further [1]. The majority of the occupying forces were stationed in camps, small forts, watchtowers, burgi and fortified bridgeheads that were built at regular intervals along the riverbank [1].

row.name: Altendorf Megalithic Tomb
row.description: The Altendorf tomb was an important megalithic tomb at Altenburg near Naumburg, northern Hesse, Germany [1]. It was a gallery grave belonging to the Late Neolithic Wartberg culture [1]. The tomb belongs to the Hessian-Westphalian stone cist group, which is part of the Wartberg culture [1]. About 4 m of the monument had been destroyed before systematic excavation took place in 1934 [1]. The tomb, oriented east-south-east to west-north-west was built into a rectangular pit of 17 x 3 m dimensions, with an entrance ramp at the east end [1]. The dead had been placed in the tomb over time, possibly over several centuries [1]. The bones indicated a minimum of 235-250 individuals [1].

row.name: The Poind and his Man
row.description: The Poind and his Man is a prehistoric site in Northumberland, England, near the village of Bolam and about 7 miles (11 km) west of Morpeth [1]. The site, consisting of a burial mound and a standing stone, is a scheduled monument [1]. The burial mound, described as a round cairn, is situated on a small knoll [1]. It dates from the Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age [1]. Its diameter is 14 metres, and it is 1.9 metres high [1]. A standing stone, height 2 metres, is next to the mound; it was formerly one of two such stones ("the poind and his man") [1]. The standing stone in the grounds of Wallington Hall is thought to have been moved from here in the early 18th century [1]. The mound was partly excavated in the 18th century by John Warburton [1].

row.name: Verziau of Gargantua
row.description: The verziau of Gargantua (or vierzeux of Gargantua), also known as Haute-Borne, is a menhir at Bois-lès-Pargny in Aisne, France [1]. The menhir is north of the town of Bois-lès-Pargny, a few meters from a small copse, near Sons-et-Ronchères [1]. At the beginning of the 19th century, the menhir had a twin sister, which was destroyed to extract a large amount of sandstone [1]. Legend has it that a man of immense size was using it to sharpen his scythe, and left the rock on the site in a gesture of anger [1]. The monument was listed as a monument historique in 1889 [1].

row.name: Howick House
row.description: The Howick house is a Mesolithic site located in Northumberland, England [1]. It was found when an amateur archaeologist noticed flint tools eroding out of a sandy cliff face near the village of Howick [1]. Investigations found a circle of substantial post holes with charcoal stains in their bases, a number of smaller stake holes, some angled in from outside a hollow, and inside the house a number of shallow hearths filled with charcoal, burnt nutshells and some fragments of bone [1]. Radiocarbon dating of the charred hazelnut shells established that the building was constructed about 7600 BC and occupied for about 100 years [1]. Some of the hearths showed signs only of nut roasting, and the numbers of shells suggested that food was cooked here in quantity, perhaps to preserve it for times of scarcity [1]. Together with the very substantial construction shown by the size of post holes, this led to the view that the house was occupied permanently rather than being used on a transient or seasonal basis as expected during the Mesolithic period [1].

row.name: Beer Quarry Caves
row.description: Beer Quarry Caves is a man-made limestone underground complex located about a mile west of the village of Beer, Devon, and the main source in England for Beer stone [1]. The tunnels resulted from 2,000 years of quarrying Beer stone, which was particularly favoured for cathedral and church features such as door and window surrounds because of its colour and workability for carving [1]. Extraction was particularly intense during the Middle Ages, but continued until the 1920s [1]. The Roman section is typified by large arches which support the roof and was hand excavated using picks and wooden wedges [1]. Beer stone was used in the Roman villa of Honeyditches, Seaton [1].

row.name: Ballyedmonduff Wedge Tomb
row.description: The Ballyedmonduff Wedge Tomb is a wedge-shaped gallery grave and a National Monument in Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown, Ireland [1]. Ballyedmonduff Wedge Tomb is found on the south-eastern slope of the Two Rock mountain [1]. The tomb was excavated in the 1830s and then again in the 1940s; during this excavation, cremated bone, a polished stone hammer, flints and pottery were found [1]. The tomb is U-shaped and features double-walling; the rectangular chamber is divided into three parts [1].

row.name: Theatre Area of Pompeii
row.description: The theatre area of Pompeii is located in the southwest region of the city [1]. There are three main buildings that make up this area: the Large Theatre, the Odeon (small theatre), and the Quadriporticum [1]. These served as an entertainment and meeting centre of the city [1]. The Large Theatre was built into a natural hill in the second century BC and was one of the first permanent stone theatres in the Roman empire [1]. It sat roughly 5,000 spectators [1]. Around 2 BC, the theatre was renovated and presented to the city of Pompeii as a gift by two relatives, M. Holconius Rufus and M. Holconius Celer, according to an inscription in the theatre [1]. The Odeon was a smaller roofed theatre, theatrum tectum, that sat 1500 spectators and was built in 80 BC [1].

row.name: Hambledon Hill
row.description: Hambledon Hill is a prehistoric hill fort in Dorset, England, in the Blackmore Vale five miles northwest of Blandford Forum [1]. The hill itself is a chalk outcrop, on the southwestern corner of Cranborne Chase, separated from the Dorset Downs by the River Stour [1]. Excavations in the 1970s and 1980s by Roger Mercer produced large quantities of Neolithic material [1]. Environmental analysis indicated the site was occupied whilst the area was still wooded with forest clearances coming later, in the Bronze Age [1]. The hillfort is a Scheduled Monument, as is the adjacent Neolithic causewayed camp [1].

row.name: Townleyhall Passage Grave
row.description: Townleyhall passage grave is a chamber tomb located around 2 km north of Dowth tomb [1]. It is part of the megalithic complex of Brú na Bóinne in County Louth, Ireland [1]. Unlike its more famous neighbours in the Boyne valley, the tomb consists of a single chamber that merges with the entrance passage making it an undifferentiated passage grave [1]. Townleyhall was excavated by George Eogan in 1962, work which found Carrowkeel ware pottery providing the first indication that Ireland's passage graves were of Neolithic date [1].

row.name: Margarita Tomb
row.description: The Margarita Tomb, also known as The Queens tomb, lies buried deep in the center of the Late Classic Acropolis of Copán [1]. It is a multi – leveled tomb with one of the largest caches ever found associated with the burial of a Maya woman [1]. Over years of excavation it was discovered that this was a tomb of a woman because of the remains found, which were covered in cinnabar and hematite [1]. Connecting the upper chamber to the lower chamber is a vaulted stairway [1]. In the lower chamber a funerary slab was found [1]. A large and multifaceted offering sat in situ (being in the original position; not having been moved) when the funerary slab was removed [1].

row.name: Aetokremnos
row.description: Aetokremnos is a rock shelter near Limassol on the southern coast of Cyprus [1]. The name means "Cliff of the eagles" in Greek [1]. Around 40 m2 have been excavated and out of the four layers documented, the third is sterile [1]. The site, which is located on a British Royal Air Force base, was discovered in 1960 by an anonymous amateur, who reported the find to Stuart Swiny [1]. Swiny noted the existence of flint artifacts and a large number of hippo bones and that much of the site had eroded into the Mediterranean [1]. Pygmy hippo bones are the most plentiful making up 74% of the bones, followed by fish remains and birds, mainly bustards [1]. The presence of fallow deer and pig is puzzling, since these animals are only thought to have been introduced in the Neolithic period [1].

row.name: Heronbridge Roman Site
row.description: Heronbridge Roman Site is the remains of a Roman settlement on both sides of Watling Street, about 2 kilometres south of Chester in Cheshire, England, with evidence of industrial activity in the late 1st and 2nd centuries [1]. The site was found by chance by a member of Chester Archaeological Society in 1929 [1]. Excavations took place in 1930–31 and found human remains with evidence of violent deaths [1]. Carbon-dating of two further skeletons, uncovered in 2004, is consistent with a date of death in the early 7th century [1]. The settlement was founded on the west bank of the River Dee in the late 1st century AD [1]. It became a significant settlement, with many established stone buildings and a quayside cut into the bedrock [1]. There are also indications of a river bridge in the area, and evidence of trade in coal (dated to about AD 200) has been found at the inland port [1]. After Roman occupation ended, around AD 350, the town decayed into ruin [1].

row.name: Tienen Mithraeum
row.description: The Tienen Mithraeum is a Mithraic temple constructed in the Belgian municipality of Tienen in the third century CE [1]. The ruins were not discovered until 1998 through excavation of the site labeled, Grijpenveld [1]. The Mithraic temple is located in the southwestern region of Tienen [1]. Beside the mithraeum is a pebble road that leads to the center of Tienen as well as a discovered tumulus, built a century before the temple [1]. From the entrance a 12-metre-long x two-metre-wide central path is found [1]. Ritual sites near the mithraeum, were found to contain nearly 14,000 animal remains [1]. A majority of these animals were pigs, sheep and chickens, killed in a juvenile state, while the other birds were killed as adults [1].

row.name: Hitzacker Archaeological Centre
row.description: The Hitzacker Archaeological Centre is an archaeological open-air museum in Hitzacker in the German state of Lower Saxony [1]. The core theme of the museum is the presentation of Bronze Age settlements [1]. The museum has three reconstructed single-room houses or longhouses that combine livestock stalls and living accommodation under one roof, a burial hut and a pit-house, as they would have looked based on local archaeological finds [1]. One of the longhouses contains an exhibition of the important aspects of life in the Bronze Age some 3,000 years ago [1]. In 1969 the first archaeological discoveries of ceramic shards and building floor plans were made during building work at Lake Hitzacker [1]. Not until 1987 were planned archaeological digs carried out on the area, because the expansion of the lake and upgrade of a federal road endangered the cultural monuments [1]. The following years yielded further finds and floor plans [1]. In 1990 the Hitzacker Archaeological Centre was founded due to the importance of these discoveries [1].

row.name: Wade's Causeway
row.description: Wade's Causeway is a Roman road, or possibly a Neolithic structure, located in the North York Moors national park in North Yorkshire, England [1]. The structure has been the subject of local folklore for several hundred years and possibly for more than a millennium [1]. Its construction was commonly attributed to a giant known as Wade, a figure from Germanic mythology [1]. The stretch of the causeway on Wheeldale Moor was cleared of vegetation and excavated in the early twentieth century by a local gamekeeper interested in archaeology [1]. The first modern written record that unquestionably relates to the Wheeldale structure was in 1720 by the antiquarian John Warburton [1].

row.name: Barpa Langass
row.description: Barpa Langass or Langass Barp is a Neolithic chambered cairn on the Isle of North Uist in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland [1]. It measures around 22 meters in diameter by 5.5 meters in height, and is around 5,000 years old [1]. The roof is constructed of two massive slabs with a third slab superimposed [1]. The entrance is at the east side [1]. The antiquary Erskine Beveridge believed that a second and perhaps a third chamber exist [1]. In or prior to 1911, Dr Beveridge excavated within and near the cairn, and he found evidence of burnt burials as well as pieces of pottery (some with patterned lines), wood ashes, burnt bones, a flint arrowhead, a scraper, and a piece of pierced talc [1].

row.name: Hartberg Megalithic Tomb
row.description: The Hartberg megalithic tomb is an archaeological site of the late Neolithic Age, near Schankweiler and about 10 kilometres south-west of Bitburg, in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany [1]. The site, on the western slope of the Hartberg north of Schankweiler, dates from around 3000 BC [1]. Bones and pottery sherds were found in the tomb, and flint knives, flint arrowheads and pottery sherds were discovered outside; these suggested a date of about 3000 BC [1]. There was a small beaker in the tomb, with "barbed-wire" decoration, of the early Bronze Age, suggesting that the site was in use, perhaps with interruptions, for around 1,000 years [1]. Slabs from the tomb were later used in the early Iron Age to build a house nearby [1].

row.name: Dog Hole Cave
row.description: Dog Hole Cave is an archaeologically significant cave near Storth, Cumbria, England [1]. Other names for the cave include Haverbrack Bank Pot, Haverbrack Dog Hole, Fairy Cave, The Dog Hole, and Doghole Cave [1]. It consists of a largely excavated 12 metres shaft formed in Carboniferous Limestone with 6 metres of steeply dipping phreatic tube at the bottom [1]. Further excavation was carried out by local scouts in the 1950s, and by researchers from Liverpool John Moores University in 2003 [1]. Radiocarbon dating of the deposits has provided dates ranging from Romano-British to Early Medieval [1].

row.name: Aymestrey Burial
row.description: The Aymestrey burial was a beaker cist at Aymestrey, Herefordshire, England [1]. While working a gravel quarry at Aymestrey, in June 1987, employees of ARC unearthed a hole with a stone lining, and human remains visible within [1]. They called in archaeologists from Hereford and Worcester County Council, who carried out an excavation and discovered a stone-lined burial pit containing the body of a child, lying on its left-hand side in a foetal position [1]. Alongside the body were an earthenware bell beaker and a flint knife [1]. The burial was dated to the Early Bronze Age [1]. The site lies between the Iron Age hill forts at Pyon Wood and Croft Ambrey, and alongside a tributary of the River Lugg [1].

row.name: Knockmany Passage Tomb
row.description: Knockmany passage tomb, or Anya's Cove, is an ancient burial monument on the summit of Knockmany Hill, near the village of Augher in County Tyrone [1]. It is the remains of a Neolithic passage tomb and its stones are decorated with rare megalithic art [1]. The monument is a passage tomb built during the Neolithic, around 3000 BC [1]. The chamber was originally covered with a stone cairn and earth [1]. The 13 sandstone orthostats remain: these are of height 3–7 feet, and three of them show carved decorations including concentric circles, spirals and zigzags [1]. They are similar to the decorated stones of the tombs at Loughcrew and Newgrange [1].

row.name: Kierikki
row.description: Kierikki is an area located in Yli-Ii by the Ii River in Finland [1]. It is about ten kilometres southeast and towards Pudasjärvi from Yli-Ii's centre [1]. Kierikki is one of Finland's most important archaeological exploration locations [1]. Excavations began around 1960 and are still ongoing [1]. Stone Age chewing gum made of birch bark was found in Kierikki’s excavations in the summer of 2007 [1].

row.name: Ħal Resqun Catacombs
row.description: The Ħal Resqun catacombs are especially notable for their carved decorations, and other features which are uncommon in Maltese catacombs [1]. The catacombs are dug into the local Globigerina Limestone [1]. The catacombs were first excavated by Temi Żammit in 1912, and again in 1934 by Żammit and his son, C. G. Żammit; although Temi Żammit reported how the site had already been disturbed in 1887 during the laying of a water main [1]. The doorway is flanked by two engraved columns, while the apsed arched entrance has carvings of a peacock and a peahen feeding a chick [1].

row.name: Stenehed
row.description: Stenehed is an Iron Age grave field located about 1 km southwest of Hällevadsholm, Munkedal Municipality, Västra Götaland County [1]. The area contains about 45 graves, a stone circle, a stone ship, and a row of menhirs [1]. Originally, there were eleven or twelve menhirs at the site; today, there are nine [1]. The tallest one is 3.3 m; the shortest - 1.4 m [1]. They are placed in a row, according to their heights [1].

row.name: Kalawan
row.description: Kalawan has a vihara monastery [1]. An inscription, recording the enshrinement of relics as a gift to the Sarvastivadin School, was found in a chaitya hall mentioning the date of "the 134th year of Azes," which corresponds to 77 CE [1]. The Kalawan monastery, together with the Dharmarajika display an original kind of architectural arrangement in which an image shrine is built opposite the entrance [1]. It is thought that this architectural pattern was initiated in the northwest and then became the prototype for the later development of monasteries with shrines in Devnimori, Ajanta, Aurangabad, Ellora, Nalanda, Ratnagiri and others [1].

row.name: Heunischenburg
row.description: The Heunischenburg is a stone fortification of the late Urnfield period near the Upper Franconian town of Kronach in Germany [1]. Its heyday was in the 9th century BC, making it the oldest stone fortification north of the Alps that is known and archaeologically investigated [1]. The fort is located on a 486-metre-high hill spur of the Wolfsberg [1]. The strong, but small fort and the many weapons found distinguish the Heunischenburg clearly from the great centres of settlement of the late Bronze Age [1]. In the first period (10th century BC) the Heunischenburg was constructed as a palisaded fortification [1]. In the second period (10th century BC) the defences were reinforced with a sandstone wall that probably burned down during a battle [1]. In the third period (9th century) the Heunischenburg was expanded into a strong hillfort [1]. The archaeological dating of the site is based on numerous bronze finds, about 70% of which are weapons [1].

row.name: Martin Down Enclosure
row.description: The Martin Down Enclosure is an archaeological site on Martin Down, near the village of Martin, in Hampshire [1]. It is near the boundaries with Dorset and Wiltshire [1]. The site is a scheduled monument, and it is one of several archaeological features on Martin Down, such as Bokerley Dyke [1]. The enclosure is the original example of a type of prehistoric feature, the "Martin Down style enclosure": they are small enclosures of the Bronze Age, area often less than 0.3 hectares, considered to be domestic settlements [1]. The rectangular enclosure has internal dimensions of about 90 metres south-west to north-east by 63 metres [1]. It has a single bank of width up to 10 metres and up to 0.7 metres above the interior, and there is an external ditch [1].

row.name: Gartnanoul
row.description: Gartnanoul is a megalithic court tomb located in Killykeen Forest Park, Loughtee Upper, County Cavan [1]. Gartnanoul is called a dual-tomb because it has two tombs both in line with each other, with each tomb having its own court [1]. It is estimated that when it was built Gartnanoul was 28 metres long and 8 metres wide [1]. The roof stones are missing although the tomb is in good condition and cairn materials are found scattered around the tomb [1].

row.name: Tievebulliagh
row.description: Tievebulliagh is a 402-metre-high mountain in the Glens of Antrim [1]. Evidence has been discovered of a Neolithic axe quarry at the foot of Tievebulliagh [1]. Flint axe heads fashioned from porcellanite that originate from this quarry have been found across the British Isles [1]. Flakes, rejects and part-finished axes have been found round the hill and peak [1]. It was here that the axes were roughed out before being finished at the sea shore [1]. They were then exported as far afield as south-west Ireland, south-east England and north-east Scotland [1].

row.name: Cromlech de Mzoura
row.description: Msoura (also Mzoura, Mezora, Mçora, M'Zorah, M'Sora or Mzora) is an archaeological site of a stone circle in northern Morocco [1]. It is located near Chouahed village, 15 kilometers southeast of Asilah, and consists of 167 monoliths surrounding a tumulus 58 m long, 54 m wide, with a height of 6 m [1]. One of the monoliths, known as El Uted measures more than 5 m, with the average height of the monoliths being 1.5 m [1]. Dated to the 4th or 3rd century BC, the site probably hints to the beginnings of the Kingdom of Mauretania [1]. Spanish archaeologist César Luis de Montalban started excavating the site in 1935 [1]. Miquel Tarradell excavated what was left of the site in the 1950s [1]. He also discovered another smaller stone ring with 16 monoliths nearby [1].

row.name: Dolmen Losa de la Mora
row.description: The Dolmen Losa de la Mora or of Rodellar is a well-preserved dolmen located in Rodellar, in the municipality of Bierge, in the Sierra de Guara (Huesca, Spain) [1]. It is at an altitude of 1,020 masl [1]. It dates from Neolithic, from around 3000 BC [1]. It consists of three orthostats covered by a large slab, which gives the dolmen its name [1]. The dolmen is surrounded by numerous stones belonging to the mound that covered it, with a diameter of dispersion of about 12 meters [1]. It was excavated by the archaeologist Martín Almagro Basch in 1935 and 1936, finding stone axes, flint tools, and skeletal remains of various individuals [1].

row.name: Yeavering Bell
row.description: Yeavering Bell is a twin-peaked hill near the River Glen in north Northumberland, England, to the west of Wooler, and forming part of the Cheviot Hills [1]. The summit, 1,158 feet (353 metres) above sea level, is encircled by the wall of a late-prehistoric hillfort, a tribal centre of the Votadini called in Brythonic and Old Welsh Din Gefron, from which the name stems [1]. The hillfort encloses an area of approximately 12 acres (4.9 ha) and is enclosed by a stone wall, upwards of 10 ft (3.0 m) thick, having four entrances, one of which is defended by a guard-house; and within this area is an inner fort, excavated out of the rock, of an oval form [1]. On the sides of the hill, and in a high valley between the Bell and the next hill, called Whitelaw, there are many remains of stone huts rudely flagged, some in groups surrounded by rampiers (ramparts), and others isolated [1]. The hillfort enclosure was constructed in two phases, according to a survey by English Heritage [1]. Yeavering Bell overlooks the important Angle site of Yeavering in the valley just to the north [1].
