row.old_value: A wellspring shrine on Hadrian's Wall dedicated to the goddess Coventina. Over 13,000 coins were thrown into the well as offerings — a Roman wishing well.
row.new_value: Dedications to Coventina and votive deposits were found in a walled area which had been built to contain the outflow from a spring now called "Coventina's Well".

row.old_value: A Roman tumuli cemetery with the tallest Roman barrow north of the Alps, standing 15 metres high. Seven grand burial mounds suggest an elite family of extraordinary wealth.
A megalithic stone circle from the 5th millennium BC in the Alentejo region. It sits in one of the densest concentrations of megalithic monuments in Western Europe.
row.new_value: The cromlech was identified in 1993 by a team of students from the University of Lisbon, led by Manuel Calado.

row.old_value: A small Roman castellum from the 1st-2nd century AD. Forts this size housed auxiliary cohorts — non-citizen soldiers recruited from the empire's edges.
row.new_value: The fort was discovered in 1894 under the direction of Heinrich Jacobi, the local section commissioner of the Imperial Limes Commission, and examined in two excavation campaigns in 1894 and 1901.

row.old_value: Two standing stones, remnants of a prehistoric cove near Beckhampton. "Adam" is a surviving piece of the avenue that once connected to Avebury.
A cylindrical limestone obelisk from the Early Neolithic with a faint spiral engraving. It was once part of a group of nine; only two survive today.
row.new_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.

row.old_value: A lake where over 150 Iron Age metal objects were thrown as offerings between 300 BC and 100 AD. The hoard includes weapons, chariot fittings, and slave chains from across Celtic Britain.
row.new_value: Llyn Cerrig Bach is a small lake located between Rhosneigr and Valley in the west of Anglesey.

row.old_value: A wedge tomb from the late Neolithic, one of about 400 scattered across the island. Wedge tombs narrow from front to back and typically face the setting sun.
row.new_value: Lisnadarragh Wedge Tomb is a prehistoric site, a wedge tomb about 16 kilometres west of Carrickmacross, in County Monaghan near the border with County Cavan.

row.old_value: A Neolithic site where objects may date to 125,000 years ago, which would make them the only known Neanderthal artifacts in the region. The claim remains controversial.
A Maya satellite city between the giants El Mirador and El Tintal, occupied from 250 to 830 AD. Extensive looting has stripped many of its structures bare.
row.new_value: The site is divided into North and South Groups, located approximately 400 metres apart.

row.old_value: Occupied 38,000 years ago during the Pleistocene, when sea levels were far lower. Stone tools from this rock shelter in Krabi document early human presence across the region.
row.new_value: The oldest use for the rock shelter was as a campground for hunters in the late Pleistocene epoch.

row.old_value: From around 10,000 BC, Aboriginal people hunted wallaby in open tundra near Kutikina Cave on the Franklin River. This Pleistocene rock shelter helped establish the antiquity of Tasmanian occupation.
row.new_value: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.

row.old_value: A 1.92-metre standing stone from around 3000 BC with petroglyphs carved into its surface. Its base was cut, so the original stone was likely even taller.
row.new_value: The Lapa de Gargantáns is a menhir located in the Galician municipality of Moraña, dated between 3000–2000 BC and discovered in 1958.

row.old_value: A Maya city from 600-830 AD caught in the war between Tikal and Calakmul. Two centuries of warfare so depleted the population that the area was abandoned.
row.new_value: Lachan K'awiil Ajaw Bot, the local La Amelia king, is depicted on La Amelia Panel 2, dated to AD 804 and continued to raise monuments at the site.

row.old_value: A Neolithic henge from 3500 BC with a circular bank 80 metres in diameter and an internal ditch. It appears mostly intact despite a reported 1908 excavation.
row.new_value: Castle Dykes Henge is a Class I Neolithic henge earthwork in the Yorkshire Dales National Park in North Yorkshire situated between the villages of Aysgarth and Thornton Rust.

row.old_value: A Neolithic burial cairn 14 m across with a 2 m standing stone beside it. This paired monument type recurs across prehistoric northern regions.
row.new_value: The Poind and his Man is a prehistoric site in Northumberland near the village of Bolam and about 7 miles west of Morpeth.

row.old_value: A 1700 BC wedge-shaped gallery grave. Wedge tombs are the most common megalithic tomb type on the island — over 500 have been recorded.
row.new_value: The tomb was excavated in the 1830s and then again in the 1940s; during this excavation, cremated bone, a polished stone hammer, flints and pottery were found.

row.old_value: A sinuous stone monument up to 6,000 years old, stretching across moorland for potentially 40 km. The visible section on Wheeldale Moor runs just over 1.6 km.
A 5,000-year-old chambered cairn 22 metres across, with a roof of two massive stone slabs. Despite partial collapse, visitors can still enter one of its burial chambers.
row.new_value: The antiquary Erskine Beveridge believed that a second and perhaps a third chamber exist.

row.old_value: A 12-meter shaft cave with finds from Roman to early medieval periods. Human and animal remains accumulated in its depths over centuries.
row.new_value: Radiocarbon dating of the deposits has provided dates ranging from Romano-British to Early Medieval.

row.old_value: A Beaker-period cist burial from 3300-2200 BC. Beaker burials placed distinctive pottery vessels with the dead — a tradition that spread across all of Western Europe.
row.new_value: While working a gravel quarry at Aymestrey, in June 1987, employees of ARC unearthed a hole with a stone lining, and human remains visible within.

row.old_value: At Taxila, this Buddhist establishment contains the largest vihara monastery in northern India. An inscription records the enshrinement of relics as a Sarvastivadin gift, dated to 77 AD.
row.new_value: An inscription, recording the enshrinement of relics as a gift to the Sarvastivadin School, was found in a chaitya hall mentioning the date of "the 134th year of Azes," which corresponds to 77 CE.

row.old_value: A Neolithic enclosure that became the type-site for a whole category of prehistoric earthwork. Archaeologists named the 'Martin Down type' after this exact monument.
row.new_value: The enclosure is the original example of a type of prehistoric feature, the "Martin Down style enclosure": they are small enclosures of the Bronze Age, area often less than 0.3 hectares.

row.old_value: A Roman town beside the modern A2 in Kent, hidden for nearly 2,000 years. A 2019 dig across 7.2 hectares exposed iron furnaces, pottery kilns, a 7-meter-wide Roman road, and a temple.
row.new_value: Watling Temple is the name given to the remains of a temple within a Roman town next to the modern A2 road in Newington, near Sittingbourne in Kent.

row.old_value: Four circular earthwork enclosures from 2500-2180 BC, each about 190 metres in diameter. Three stand in a nearly straight line, with the fourth offset by 350 metres.
row.new_value: Priddy Circles are a linear arrangement of four circular earthwork enclosures near the village of Priddy on the Mendip Hills in Somerset.

row.old_value: A limestone cave housing Neanderthal fossils from around 47,000 BC. The remains of over a dozen individuals include evidence of cannibalism.
row.new_value: The first sequencing of the Neanderthal Y chromosome was successfully completed from a specimen from Sidrón Cave.

row.old_value: A Roman gravity dam near Mérida dated to the 1st or 2nd century AD that still holds water. Its earth-and-concrete construction has endured nearly 2,000 years of continuous use.
row.new_value: The Cornalvo Dam is a Roman gravity dam built to supply water to the Roman colonia of Emerita Augusta, capital of the Roman province of Lusitania.

row.old_value: 1st–2nd c. AD public baths buried beneath the old city. Hypocaust heating, three bathing halls, and a Greek marble statue of a dancing satyr found during 1986 excavations.
row.new_value: As regards chronology, the remains correspond to a period between the end of the 1st century and mid-2nd century CE.

row.old_value: Pompeii had permanent stone theatres decades before Rome built its first. The Large Theatre seated 5,000 and was carved into a natural hillside.
row.new_value: The Large Theatre was built into a natural hill in the second century BC and was one of the first permanent stone theatres in the Roman empire.

row.old_value: About twenty menhirs and monoliths on a wooded hilltop, the tallest standing 4 metres high. Whether this is a dolmen or a cromlech remains an open question.
row.new_value: On a wooded hill above Odrinhas stand the menhirs of the Barreira Megalithic Complex; no carved symbols have been detected, save a few pairs of small circular cavities, possibly eyes.

row.old_value: An oval-shaped broch from 150 BC that originally stood on a freshwater lake island. Walls survive 4.5 metres high, and the sea now laps at its foundations.
row.new_value: Now on an exposed promontory of South Uist, but originally on a freshwater lake, the oval Iron Age broch of Dun Vulan still has walls standing 4.5 metres high and 4 metres wide.
On the right bank of the Nakhchivançay, excavations at Uzun oba in 2015 brought to light painted ceramic pieces from the V millennium BC, finds that are very rare for the region.

row.old_value: Less than 3 km from Stonehenge, built beside the ceremonial Stonehenge Avenue, this ~800 BC hillfort has the River Avon as its southern boundary — a naturally defensible position on three sides.
row.new_value: Less than 3 kilometres from Stonehenge, the Iron Age hillfort of Vespasian's Camp carries a Roman general's name, given in the 16th century, yet no evidence suggests he ever came here.

row.old_value: A Bronze Age landscape and Medieval structure uncovered during housing construction in 2013. Decorated tile foundations had lain completely unknown just below the surface.
row.new_value: Before 500 new houses were built near Wellington, digs in 2013 found the unknown Longforth Farm: stone foundations around courtyards, their decorated floor tiles like Glastonbury Abbey's.

row.old_value: A burial site where a rectangular stone coffin was found during Japanese-era rule. Giant stone piles and artifacts date to the 2nd millennium BC.
The oldest use for the rock shelter was as a campground for hunters in the late Pleistocene epoch.
row.new_value: Late Pleistocene hunters first camped at Lang Rongrien Rock Shelter. Its layers hold charcoal, stone flakes and animal bones, the oldest charcoal dated to around 39,000 years ago.

row.old_value: An Iron Age village with a fogou (underground passage) whose function is still debated. Stone huts replaced timber ones around 200 BC and remained in use for centuries.
row.new_value: Just below the ground at Carn Euny in Cornwall runs a fogou, an underground passage more than 65 feet long roofed with massive stone slabs. The remains of stone huts are still visible.

row.old_value: A mountaintop site at 3,580 metres with cave paintings and stone burial towers called chullpas. These above-ground tombs let Andean peoples keep their ancestors visible on the landscape.
row.new_value: High on a Peruvian mountain, 3,580 metres up, Markahirka keeps cave paintings and stone tombs, and looks out over the Puchka valley to the towns of Huari and Huachis.

row.old_value: Begun around 300 BC and abandoned unfinished by 275 BC, this large peristyle served briefly as Athens' law courts before being demolished for material reused in South Stoa II.
row.new_value: On the east side of the Agora of Athens, the Square Peristyle was begun around 300 BC but never finished. It probably served as law courts; the Stoa of Attalos rose on its foundations.

row.old_value: A Neolithic necropolis from the 4th millennium BC with burial chambers cut into solid rock. These artificial caves mimic natural cave burials but in controlled, purpose-built spaces.
row.new_value: Cut into marlstone with stone tools, the Artificial Caves of Alapraia end in round chambers under skylights, believed to have let bodies in when the corridors could no longer be used.

row.old_value: A 420 km stretch of Roman frontier fortifications along the Danube, defended from the time of Augustus to the 5th century AD. Forts lined the river at regular intervals.
row.new_value: Along the riverbank ran the Pannonian Limes, a Roman frontier of camps, watchtowers and fortified bridgeheads that guarded the Pannonian provinces against attacks from the north.

row.old_value: The Poind and his Man is a prehistoric site in Northumberland near the village of Bolam and about 7 miles west of Morpeth.
row.new_value: On a small knoll in Northumberland, The Poind and his Man joins a round cairn to a standing stone 2 metres tall; a stone at Wallington Hall is thought to have been moved from here.

row.old_value: A 4.35-meter sandstone monolith at Bois-lès-Pargny, dating to around 3500 BC. A twin menhir was demolished for building material in the 19th century; legend links both stones to the giant Gargantua.
row.new_value: Legend says a man of immense size sharpened his scythe on the Verziau of Gargantua and left it here in anger. The menhir's twin sister was destroyed for its sandstone.

row.old_value: A 2,000-year-old underground quarry that supplied stone for cathedrals across the region. The soft limestone was prized for its carvability in door and window surrounds.
row.new_value: 2,000 years of quarrying hollowed out Beer Quarry Caves in Devon. In the Roman section, cut by hand with picks and wooden wedges, large arches still hold up the limestone roof.

row.old_value: A Neolithic and Bronze Age cemetery from 3300-800 BC with clusters of round barrows. Each mound held individual burials — a shift from the earlier communal tomb tradition.
row.new_value: On Codford Down, only a bell barrow and five of ten bowl barrows survive at the Aston Valley Barrow Cemetery, where digs revealed Bronze Age and some possible Saxon urned cremations.

row.old_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.
row.new_value: On a hill just outside Portelas, the limestone Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo bears a faint spiral-like engraving. Early Neolithic, it was not funerary, and the end it served is still debated.

row.old_value: A Roman Danubian fort (134 x 126 m) in the Moesian Limes frontier system. Its walls were upgraded from wood to stone before Domitian's Dacian War in 87 AD.
Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.
row.new_value: On the Franklin River in Tasmania lies Kutikina Cave, the most southerly human occupation in the world during the last ice age, with evidence of wallaby hunting on open tundra.

row.old_value: A decorated Iron Age bronze shield from ~400 BC, found in a river alongside a sword fragment lodged in a human skull. The shield's La Tene metalwork is exquisite.
row.new_value: Found in the River Witham in 1826, the Witham Shield is Iron Age bronze of La Tène style. Small rivet holes and stains hint at a long-legged leather wild boar once riveted to its face.

row.old_value: Dating to 3000 BC, this Funnelbeaker dolmen near Keitum was moved stone by stone in 1954 when an airport displaced it. Of roughly 600 such graves once on this island, half survive.
row.new_value: In 1954, while Sylt Airport was under development, the stones of the Harhoog were moved to the coast near Keitum: a Funnelbeaker dolmen whose graves probably date to around 3000 BC.

row.old_value: A Neolithic gallery grave from 3400 BC that contained an unusually large number of burials. Wartberg culture tombs like this were communal ossuaries for whole communities.
row.new_value: Over time, possibly over several centuries, the dead were laid in the Altendorf Megalithic Tomb, a Late Neolithic gallery grave in northern Hesse. Its bones speak of at least 235-250 people.

row.old_value: A Neolithic hilltop with paired causewayed enclosures from around 3500 BC, later converted into an Iron Age hillfort. Skeletons with arrowheads suggest violent attack.
row.new_value: Hambledon Hill, a chalk outcrop in Dorset, bears a prehistoric hill fort beside a Neolithic causewayed camp, occupied while the area was still wooded, before the Bronze Age clearances.

row.old_value: Early Christian catacombs at Gudja with carvings so unusual they provoke debate: some historians classify them as paleochristian; others question whether the Christian markers are conclusive.
row.new_value: Dug into Globigerina Limestone, the Ħal Resqun Catacombs open through an arched entrance carved with a peacock and a peahen feeding a chick, its doorway flanked by two engraved columns.

row.old_value: A rare dual court tomb — two megalithic tombs sharing a single mound, each with its own ceremonial court. Once 28 metres long, its roof stones have all collapsed.
row.new_value: In Killykeen Forest Park lies Gartnanoul, a megalithic dual tomb: two tombs in line, each with its own court, an estimated 28 metres long when built. Its roof stones are missing.

At Bartlow Hills the tallest barrow rises 15 metres, the largest Roman barrow north of the Alps. Excavators found walled graves with cremains in glass vessels, kept in large wooden chests.

row.old_value: A ruined megalithic temple with a typical two-apse plan and paved court. Coastal erosion was believed to have destroyed it, but 2015 investigations found the remains intact.
row.new_value: Built between 3600 and 3000 BC and thought largely lost to coastal erosion, Xrobb l-Għaġin Temple survives, as 2015 investigations revealed, with an unrecorded megalithic structure nearby.

row.old_value: 600-909 AD Maya settlement in Petén with three groups of platforms on a north-south axis. Group A's pyramid stands over 10 m tall in a wooded hilltop — largely unexcavated.
row.new_value: On a wooded hilltop in Petén, a Maya pyramid over 10 metres high rises among the collapsed structures of El Temblor, and a damaged stela still stands to its east.

row.old_value: Hill fort at Bugojno, first inhabited 2500-1700 BC, abandoned for four centuries, then reoccupied in the Iron Age until the 3rd century BC. Its strata defined a late Bronze Age cultural group.
row.new_value: About 40 metres above the river Poričnica, the hill fort of Pod yielded the stratified materials that defined the Central Bosnian cultural group of the late Bronze Age.

row.old_value: An Olmec site from 1100–800 BC famous for two pairs of monumental sculptures found intact and undisturbed. Twin figures sit between crouching jaguars.
row.new_value: Beside a pyramid-hill in Veracruz, El Azuzul kept two pairs of Olmec sculptures intact and apparently undisturbed since Pre-Classic times, among them two nearly identical seated figures.

row.old_value: Iron Age burial mounds from the 6th century BC containing elite wagon burials with gold jewelry and imported Greek and Etruscan luxury goods.
row.new_value: In the Graves of Sainte-Colombe-sur-Seine, burial mounds of the 6th century BC, a woman was laid to rest on an iron-clad funerary wagon, gold bracelets and earrings in her grave.

row.old_value: The Lapa de Gargantáns is a menhir located in the Galician municipality of Moraña, dated between 3000–2000 BC and discovered in 1958.
row.new_value: Petroglyphs are engraved on the Lapa de Gargantáns, a menhir in Moraña dated between 3000–2000 BC. Its exact function is unknown; some link it to burials, worship or old tribal boundaries.

row.old_value: A Harappan-era mound from 3300-1300 BC with a hamlet surrounded by stone defensive walls. Pottery, copper objects, and figurines of bulls and birds were found inside.
row.new_value: Ali Murad Mound lies 20 miles southwest of Dadu. At its top, an ancient hamlet was found ringed by defensive walls of stone blocks, and N. G. Majumdar explored and named the site.

row.old_value: Over 9 km of ditches and ramparts enclosing 300 hectares, built in the early Roman era. Venutius or Cartimandua — or both before their split after 51 AD — held this North Yorkshire stronghold.
row.new_value: Over 9 kilometres of ditches and ramparts form the Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications, where Wheeler found an Iron Age sword in its ash wood scabbard and, nearby, the skull of a severed head.

row.old_value: Ruins of a Roman fish-salting factory and baths from the 1st century AD. Garum production was big business — the Roman appetite for fish sauce was enormous.
row.new_value: Above Creiro Beach in the Arrábida Natural Park, the Roman Ruins of Creiro keep baths and a fish-salting factory, its salted fish and fish sauces exported throughout the Empire in amphorae.

row.old_value: Around 500 AD. Buried deep in Copán's Late Classic acropolis, the Margarita Tomb held one of the largest caches ever found with a Maya woman's burial — she was almost certainly royalty.
row.new_value: Buried deep in the Late Classic Acropolis of Copán, the Margarita Tomb held a Maya woman's remains covered in cinnabar and hematite, a vaulted stairway joining its upper and lower chambers.

row.old_value: A Roman settlement with stone buildings and a quayside cut into bedrock. Industrial furnaces from the 1st century show it was a manufacturing hub, not just a town.
row.new_value: Found by chance in 1929 on the River Dee, the Heronbridge Roman Site had stone buildings and a quayside cut into the bedrock. Digs found human remains with evidence of violent deaths.

row.old_value: The only Neolithic gallery grave of its type in the entire region, dating to about 3000 BC. Two sandstone-slab chambers were built into the slope of the Hartberg.
row.new_value: From around 3000 BC, the Hartberg Megalithic Tomb held bones and a small beaker that suggests use, perhaps with interruptions, for around 1,000 years. Iron Age builders took its slabs.

row.old_value: The oldest known stone fortification north of the Alps, dating to the 9th century BC. It guarded a Bronze Age copper and tin trade route through the mountains.
row.new_value: On a hill spur near Kronach, the Heunischenburg is the oldest known and investigated stone fortification north of the Alps. Its sandstone wall probably burned down during a battle.

row.old_value: Dedications to Coventina and votive deposits were found in a walled area which had been built to contain the outflow from a spring now called "Coventina's Well".
row.new_value: A walled spring called Coventina's Well held 13,487 coins, a relief of three water nymphs and altars to the goddess Coventina, some showing her reclining and partially clothed.

row.old_value: Llyn Cerrig Bach is a small lake located between Rhosneigr and Valley in the west of Anglesey.
row.new_value: In 1942, as peat was dug for a runway extension, over 150 Iron Age metal objects surfaced at Llyn Cerrig Bach, apparently votive offerings. The first was an iron gang chain for slaves.

row.old_value: Watling Temple is the name given to the remains of a temple within a Roman town next to the modern A2 road in Newington, near Sittingbourne in Kent.
row.new_value: A 2019 dig at Newington in Kent rediscovered a Roman town of iron furnaces and pottery kilns, the temple now called Watling Temple, and a 7 metres wide road older than Watling Street.

row.old_value: A Talaiotic settlement from the 2nd millennium BC featuring a talaiot tower 12 metres across on the outside but only 6 inside. Walls this thick were built to last.
row.new_value: Until 2016 and 2017, bushes and trees covered Na Nova on Mallorca. Its talaiot, a megalithic tower 12 metres across, still keeps its polylithic column and an entrance under a stone lintel.

row.old_value: A Roman villa built inside the ramparts of a larger Iron Age fortress. A bath suite with mosaic floors was among the rooms uncovered during 19th-century excavations.
row.new_value: Within the ramparts of an Iron Age fortress near Daventry lies Borough Hill Roman Villa, a single storey of marlstone rooms running from north to south, a bath suite among them.

row.old_value: The largest and heaviest prehistoric standing stone in Cornwall, weighing 16.5 tonnes. Made of Devonian shale with striking feldspar veining.
row.new_value: On the summit of St Breock Downs stands the St Breock Downs Monolith, the largest and heaviest prehistoric menhir in Cornwall, around 16.5 tonnes of shale set among quartz pebbles.

row.old_value: The largest surviving group of Roman barrows in Britain, from the 1st–2nd century AD. Six burial mounds line the old Great North Road.
row.new_value: For almost two thousand years, travellers along the Roman road that eventually became the Great North Road have passed Six Hills, a collection of Roman barrows in Stevenage, Hertfordshire.

row.old_value: As regards chronology, the remains correspond to a period between the end of the 1st century and mid-2nd century CE.
row.new_value: High above the River Tagus lie the ruins of the Roman Baths of Toledo, assumed from their scale to be public, part of the system that brought clean water to Toletum by aqueduct.

row.old_value: A long storage building from the age of Pericles, used to warehouse imported grain — mainly barley and wheat. It fed the Athenian navy based at the nearby port.
row.new_value: Built in the time of Pericles, the long Makra Stoa stored imported barley and wheat for Athens, supplied its fleet of triremes and, in times of shortage, fed the people directly.

row.old_value: Castle Dykes Henge is a Class I Neolithic henge earthwork in the Yorkshire Dales National Park in North Yorkshire situated between the villages of Aysgarth and Thornton Rust.
row.new_value: In the Yorkshire Dales, Castle Dykes Henge draws a roughly circular Neolithic bank around an internal ditch. Excavation was reported in 1908, yet the henge appears to be mostly intact.

row.old_value: Post holes, hearths, and charred hazelnut shells mark this Northumberland cliff camp, dated to 7600 BC. Structural evidence points to repeated seasonal occupation over many generations.
row.new_value: Flint tools eroding from a sandy cliff revealed Howick House: a circle of post holes, hearths of burnt nutshells, a home built about 7600 BC and occupied for about 100 years.

row.old_value: A Neolithic passage grave near the Boyne Valley megaliths. Unlike its famous neighbors, this tomb started as a settlement that was converted into a burial site.
row.new_value: Around 2 km north of Dowth lies Townleyhall Passage Grave, one chamber merging with its passage. Its Carrowkeel ware gave the first indication that Ireland's passage graves were Neolithic.

row.old_value: An 11th-millennium BC rock shelter containing burned bones of pygmy hippos alongside human tools. If the link holds, humans drove these mini-hippos to extinction.
row.new_value: At Aetokremnos, the Cliff of the eagles near Limassol, pygmy hippo bones make up 74% of the bones in the rock shelter. Yet fallow deer and pig lie there too, and their presence is puzzling.

row.old_value: Radiocarbon dating of the deposits has provided dates ranging from Romano-British to Early Medieval.
row.new_value: Some call it Fairy Cave: Dog Hole Cave near Storth is a shaft of 12 metres in Carboniferous Limestone, ending in a steep phreatic tube, where local scouts dug in the 1950s.

row.old_value: While working a gravel quarry at Aymestrey, in June 1987, employees of ARC unearthed a hole with a stone lining, and human remains visible within.
row.new_value: In June 1987, quarry workers found a stone-lined pit: the Aymestrey Burial, a child in a foetal position with a bell beaker and a flint knife, from the Early Bronze Age.

row.old_value: Stones on Knockmany Hill's summit are carved with spirals and concentric circles — rare megalithic art in a monument dated to 3000 BC. A concrete shelter built in 1959 now protects the carved slabs.
row.new_value: On the summit of Knockmany Hill, the Knockmany Passage Tomb was built around 3000 BC. Of its 13 sandstone orthostats, three bear carved concentric circles, spirals and zigzags.

row.old_value: The enclosure is the original example of a type of prehistoric feature, the "Martin Down style enclosure": they are small enclosures of the Bronze Age, area often less than 0.3 hectares.
row.new_value: A single bank and an external ditch frame the Martin Down Enclosure in Hampshire, the original example of the small Bronze Age enclosures considered to be domestic settlements.

row.old_value: A twin-peaked Iron Age hillfort enclosing 4.9 hectares, the tribal center of the Votadini. Its stone wall encircles the summit at 353 meters above sea level.
row.new_value: A stone wall upwards of 10 ft thick encircles the summit of Yeavering Bell, a twin-peaked hill where the Votadini had a tribal centre. Remains of stone huts are scattered over its sides.

row.old_value: Maya site 350 BC-250 AD in the Peten Basin. Teotihuacano imagery on La Sufricaya stelae and murals suggests foreign or non-Maya occupation, a rare contact between distant Mesoamerican cultures.
row.new_value: In the Petén Basin, the Maya site of La Sufricaya lies approximately 1.2 km west of Holmul, and how the two sites related in the Classic period is still being investigated.

row.old_value: The fort was discovered in 1894 under the direction of Heinrich Jacobi, the local section commissioner of the Imperial Limes Commission, and examined in two excavation campaigns in 1894 and 1901.
row.new_value: Am Forsthofweg, a Roman fortlet on the Limes, is an almost square earthwork whose only gate faced north. Inside, a wooden construction of around 45 square meters was found, its use unknown.

row.old_value: A Roman fish farm from 146 BC with a connecting aqueduct carved into coastal rock. Romans engineered saltwater ponds to breed fish on an industrial scale.
row.new_value: East of Santa Eulària des Riu on Ibiza, S'Argamassa Roman Fish Farm keeps remains of rectangular tanks where garum once fermented, before amphoras carried it to all parts of the empire.

row.old_value: Priddy Circles are a linear arrangement of four circular earthwork enclosures near the village of Priddy on the Mendip Hills in Somerset.
row.new_value: On the Mendip Hills lie the Priddy Circles, four earthwork rings 185 to 194 m across, probable Neolithic ritual monuments. Three form a nearly straight line; the fourth strays to the north.

row.old_value: Royal estate of Inca emperor Huayna Capac, built 1464–1525 AD in the Sacred Valley at 2,910 metres. Such estates concentrated wealth in the emperor's bloodline and served as fortified country palaces.
row.new_value: Fitted stonework, gatehouses and the foundation of a great hall mark Quispiguanca, royal estate of the Inca emperor Huayna Capac, taken by Francisco Pizarro as his encomienda in the 1530s.

row.old_value: Two Bronze Age standing stones, each about 3 metres tall but only 20 cm thick. They stand 3 metres apart like thin blades driven into the earth.
row.new_value: Two slender stones, each about 3 m high yet only about 20 cm thick, stand on Holy Island: the Penrhos Feilw Standing Stones, thought to be Bronze Age, their origins and purpose unclear.

row.old_value: Megalithic temples from 3700-2500 BC overlooking the Grand Harbour. Originally three temple complexes, but only one survives today.
row.new_value: On a plateau above the Grand Harbour, the Kordin Temples keep a stone-paved forecourt found in no other temple of Malta. The first part is believed to have been built around 3700 BC.

row.old_value: A small Neolithic stone circle also known as The Druid's Temple. An Early Christian site lies nearby, layering pagan and Christian sacred space.
row.new_value: Today only four upright stones of the original nine remain at Templebryan Stone Circle, The Druid's Temple. Nearby, a small ruined church stands beside a stone with a bullaun.

row.old_value: A defended Iron Age settlement first built between the 7th and 5th centuries BC. Enclosures like these housed several round timber buildings inside.
row.new_value: On a Northumberland hillside, the Slate Hill Settlement shields the north and west of its Iron Age enclosure with four concentric ramparts of stone and earth; a steep slope guards the south.

row.old_value: Occupying a hilltop in Loznica district, this Roman town's ancient name — Gensis — has never been confirmed. Below the walls, a harbour operated on the river Drina.
row.new_value: Koviljkin grad crowns a hilltop: ruins of a Roman town that may have been named Gensis, a name never confirmed. The Drina once flowed below, where a river harbour is believed to have been.

row.old_value: An unexcavated coastal broch with views to Foula, Vaila, and Fair Isle. A massive triangular lintel stone still sits over the entrance despite centuries of collapse.
row.new_value: On a steep knoll near Shetland's cliffs and sea, the unexcavated Broch of Culswick keeps a massive triangular lintel stone over its entrance, the passage behind it nearly filled with debris.

row.old_value: The Cornalvo Dam is a Roman gravity dam built to supply water to the Roman colonia of Emerita Augusta, capital of the Roman province of Lusitania.
row.new_value: The Cornalvo Dam, a Roman gravity dam of the 1st–2nd century AD, was built to supply water to Emerita Augusta, capital of Lusitania, and belongs to the Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida.

row.old_value: 3rd-century AD Mithraic temple, one of only four mithraea found here. Undiscovered until 1998, its ritual pit yielded feasting remains revealing the secret banqueting rites of the Mithraic cult.
row.new_value: Unearthed only in 1998, the Tienen Mithraeum was a Mithraic temple of the third century CE. Ritual sites nearby held nearly 14,000 animal remains, mostly young pigs, sheep and chickens.

On the North York Moors lies Wade's Causeway, a Roman road or possibly a Neolithic structure. For centuries folklore credited its building to Wade, a giant from Germanic mythology.

row.old_value: An Iron Age grave field with 45 burials, a stone ship, and menhirs arranged by height—tallest to shortest. The gradient is deliberate.
row.new_value: Nine menhirs stand in a row at Stenehed, placed by height from 3.3 m to 1.4 m, beside about 45 graves, a stone circle and a stone ship of the Iron Age. Once there were eleven or twelve.

row.old_value: An inscription, recording the enshrinement of relics as a gift to the Sarvastivadin School, was found in a chaitya hall mentioning the date of "the 134th year of Azes," which corresponds to 77 CE.
row.new_value: At Kalawan, an image shrine faces the monastery entrance, a plan thought to have become the prototype for monasteries at Ajanta, Ellora and Nalanda. A relic inscription dates to 77 CE.

row.old_value: A dolmen with three orthostats capped by a large slab at 1,020 meters altitude. At 3000 BC, Neolithic people hauled megaliths to mountaintop burial sites.
row.new_value: In the Sierra de Guara, the Dolmen Losa de la Mora rests a large slab on three orthostats, from around 3000 BC. Excavators found stone axes, flint tools and the bones of several people.

row.old_value: A timber circle from 2049 BC with an upturned oak tree root at its centre. The upside-down tree may symbolise a world turned on its head — death itself.
row.new_value: Near Old Hunstanton in Norfolk stood Seahenge: 55 split oak trunks around an upturned tree root, built in the spring-summer of 2049 BC, one trunk with a narrow Y fork permitting access.

row.old_value: The cromlech was identified in 1993 by a team of students from the University of Lisbon, led by Manuel Calado.
row.new_value: In the Alentejo, 34 granite menhirs of the Vale Maria do Meio Cromlech form an east-west arch, and two of them bear engravings of circles, horseshoes and lunar crescents.
In Avebury parish stand The Longstones, Adam and Eve. Adam, an estimated 62 tons, fell over in 1911 and was re-erected in 1912; close by lay a Beaker burial of a middle-aged man.

row.old_value: An Iron Age warrior buried with an exceptional set of grave goods, including a unique helmet. He was about 45, stood 1.72 metres tall, and was buried with full military honors.
row.new_value: Found in 2008, the North Bersted Man was a warrior buried in the first century BC with an exceptional set of objects, his helmet adorned with two crests that once ran down its back.

row.old_value: Lisnadarragh Wedge Tomb is a prehistoric site, a wedge tomb about 16 kilometres west of Carrickmacross, in County Monaghan near the border with County Cavan.
row.new_value: In County Monaghan, near the Cavan border, Lisnadarragh Wedge Tomb is walled by 20 orthostats that shrink from south-west to north-east, the largest, at the entrance, 1.8 metres high.

row.old_value: Dating 4200–2500 BC, this pictograph on Hisingen island is the southernmost rock painting in the country — and among the rarest, with fewer than a handful known from the western provinces.
row.new_value: On a steep cliff on Hisingen, red ochre bonded with the rock still shows ships, fish, a large deer and wave-like patterns: the Tumlehed Rock Painting, the southernmost recorded in Sweden.

row.old_value: A pre-Columbian site with gold offerings and evidence of human sacrifice in its burials. Radiocarbon dates place the main occupation between 200 and 900 AD.
row.new_value: Bulldozing topsoil in 1948, the U.S. Navy struck Venado Beach: the remains of 369 individuals, many burials in ceramic urns, gold offerings and evidence for human sacrifice.

row.old_value: Dating to 3500–2800 BC on Møn near Klekkende, this passage grave has a chamber and connecting passage. Its kerbstones are among the tallest at any comparable Neolithic monument.
row.new_value: On the island of Møn, two entrance passages, almost parallel and facing east, lead into Klekkende Høj. Inside lay human remains, flint weapons, clay vessels and amber jewellery.

row.old_value: Bronze Age hypogeum from 1700–1500 BC cut into Mallorcan limestone. Oval and rectangular chambers with benches and niches once held copper daggers, flint knives, and impressed ceramics.
row.new_value: On Mallorca lies a set of Bronze Age caves, the Hypogeum of Cala Sant Vicenç. Eight caves are visible today, yet when Wilfrid James Hemp studied them, there were fifteen.

row.old_value: A 4th-century BC burial mound that yielded a stunning gold wreath, silver vessels, and a complete horse harness with silver fittings. One intact tomb held a chariot and a sacrificed horse.
row.new_value: In the center of Vratsa, the Mogilan Mound kept one stone tomb intact. In its chamber lay a gold wreath, earrings and a gilded silver knee pad showing the great mother goddess.

row.old_value: A hilltop with a summit cairn whose surrounding peat has been dated to around 1500 BC. The uniformly aged peat suggests the cairn was built when the hilltop was freshly cleared.
row.new_value: On the Howden Moors, peat near the summit cairn of Margery Hill is uniformly about 3,500 years old, a sign it was built, not natural: believed part of a Bronze Age burial mound.

row.old_value: A Proto-Norse runestone from 200-450 AD, inscribed in Elder Futhark runes. It may be the oldest written record of burial rites and inheritance in its region.
row.new_value: Found in 1627 in a churchyard wall, the Tune Stone carries Proto-Norse runes from circa 200–450 AD, possibly the oldest Norwegian attestation of burial rites, inheritance and beer.

row.old_value: From Seaton in Devon to Dover in Kent, with finds dated to 600–450 BC and use stretching back to the Stone Age. Its eastern segment was rebranded the Pilgrims' Way in the 19th century.
row.new_value: From Seaton to Dover ran the Harrow Way, an ancient trackway dated to 600 to 450 BC but probably in existence since the Stone Age. Its eastern part was later known as the Pilgrims' Way.

row.old_value: The Large Theatre was built into a natural hill in the second century BC and was one of the first permanent stone theatres in the Roman empire.
row.new_value: In the Theatre Area of Pompeii, a Large Theatre built into a hill in the second century BC seated roughly 5,000 spectators, one of the first permanent stone theatres in the Roman empire.

row.old_value: An open-air museum with reconstructed Bronze Age longhouses where livestock and humans shared a single roof. A burial hut and pit-house complete the village.
row.new_value: In 1969, building work at Lake Hitzacker turned up ceramic shards. The Hitzacker Archaeological Centre shows reconstructed Bronze Age longhouses with stalls and living space under one roof.

row.old_value: The antiquary Erskine Beveridge believed that a second and perhaps a third chamber exist.
row.new_value: On North Uist stands Barpa Langass, a Neolithic chambered cairn around 5,000 years old, roofed with massive slabs. Erskine Beveridge believed a second, perhaps a third, chamber exists.

row.old_value: A Neolithic settlement from 3500-3100 BC that overturned views of Stone Age life in the far north. People here were not nomads -- they lived in permanent villages.
row.new_value: By the Ii River lies Kierikki, where excavations began around 1960 and are still ongoing. In the summer of 2007 the diggers found Stone Age chewing gum made of birch bark.

row.old_value: A Neolithic axe quarry producing porcellanite tools traded across the British Isles. Axes from this mountain have surfaced from the Outer Hebrides to the south coast.
row.new_value: At the foot of Tievebulliagh in the Glens of Antrim lay a Neolithic axe quarry. Porcellanite axes roughed out here were finished at the sea shore and found across the British Isles.

row.old_value: A 167-monolith stone circle surrounding a 58-meter tumulus. One stone called "El Uted" stands over 5 meters tall — towering above the rest.
row.new_value: 167 monoliths ring a tumulus at Cromlech de Mzoura, El Uted among them at more than 5 m. Dated to the 4th or 3rd century BC, it probably hints at the dawn of the Kingdom of Mauretania.

Taliata was a Roman fort on the Moesian Limes, the chain of forts along the Danube. Domitian gave its wood and earth walls stone faces in 87 AD; an early Christian basilica was found there.
In Dulan Village, the Dulan Site holds a rectangular stony coffin, dug during Japanese rule, and a giant stone pile found by Academia Sinica. Its objects date back to 3,000 years ago.

row.old_value: Taliata was a Roman fort on the Moesian Limes, the chain of forts along the Danube. Domitian gave its wood and earth walls stone faces in 87 AD; an early Christian basilica was found there.
In Dulan Village, the Dulan Site holds a rectangular stony coffin, dug during Japanese rule, and a giant stone pile found by Academia Sinica. Its objects date back to 3,000 years ago.
